name: Alabama Reflector
title: Commentary: Doug Jones did what he had to do
description: The phrase “moral victory” can inspire hard eye rolls. It’s understandable. Victory is holding power and enacting an agenda. Not watching government go on without you. So saying something constructive about Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones could feel like invoking that dreaded pair of words. Elections create winners and runners-up. Politicians wor[...]
text:
A lectern with a campaign sign for Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones sits before a speech from Jones in Birmingham, Alabama on Nov. 3, 2026. Jones lost the election to Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville but had the best finish in the race of any Democrat since 2002. (Andi Rice for Alabama Reflector)The phrase “moral victory” can inspire hard eye rolls.
It’s understandable. Victory is holding power and enacting an agenda. Not watching government go on without you.
So saying something constructive about Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones could feel like invoking that dreaded pair of words. Elections create winners and runners-up. Politicians work to be the former and not the latter.
Jones’ campaign ended in defeat Tuesday to Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville. In his concession statement Wednesday, the former U.S. senator said that growing the Alabama Democratic Party was one of his priorities in the race.
“We brought new people into the political process and helped lay the groundwork for Democrats to compete in elections for years to come,” he said. “And the results across Alabama give us a lot to celebrate.”
In other elections, one might dismiss this talk as a salve on a wound. But Jones is correct. His campaign filled the huge crater left by the Democrats’ disastrous 2022 campaign, leaving a foundation the party can build on.
And make no mistake. The 2022 Democratic campaign was a catastrophe. The party seemingly forgot to recruit statewide candidates. The Democratic ticket that year featured a lot of first-time candidates and amateurs, none of whom had name recognition. Their gubernatorial nominee had no resources and got an anemic 29% of the vote.
A Democrat losing a statewide race in Alabama is normal. But the candidates couldn’t motivate Democratic voters. And that affected local races. Several legislators in what should have been safely Democratic Black Belt seats found themselves in tighter-than-normal races with Republican challengers. 
If that had happened again this year, I would probably be writing about the extinction of the Alabama Democratic Party. 
But it didn’t.
Black southerners came out in force after the U.S. Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais and the Republican-controlled Alabama Legislature redrew Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District to favor a Republican. U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, tapped into this anger and managed to hold onto his seat, while holding down Republican margins in the Wiregrass, a key region for the Alabama GOP. 
But a single U.S. House district cannot stand in for the state. That’s where Jones came in.
The nominee united Democrats who revere the former U.S. senator for his 2017 victory over former Alabama Chief Justice Roy Moore. In a state where leaders demonize minorities at a whim, Jones called for inclusiveness. He delivered a clear message about affordability and accountability and saw no conflict between the two. 
Jones pushed to repeal the grocery tax. He said he would appoint a secretary of energy to address the state’s high residential energy prices. Jones also vowed to address the ongoing humanitarian disaster in Alabama’s prisons.
And he showed some ruthlessness. Jones repeatedly highlighted his plan for a one-year moratorium on data centers, an issue that cut across party lines. He attacked Tuberville over the Republican’s baffling, weekslong insistence that data center critics were stooges of the Chinese Communist Party, forcing Tuberville to back down from his missionary work for the facilities (albeit in back-and-forth ways that should leave people wondering where he actually stands).
Jones also seemed far more interested in the people he wanted to govern than Tuberville. The campaign estimated that he held 20 town halls around the state that drew hundreds and sometimes thousands of people, even in deep-red areas. Jones made himself available for all kinds of questions, a politician not afraid of scrutiny.
In the end, Jones fell short. The hole for Democrats was large. Tuberville had too much money. The GOP still gets juice from straight-ticket voting and white rural resistance to Democrats.
And yet, his campaign was not a failure.
A 67% to 29% GOP victory in 2022 became a 52% to 48% one. A 413,000-vote total nearly doubled to over 806,000. A party that could have lost its core legislative districts in 2022 flipped four seats, the best results for Democrats in decades. After years of teasing the party, Huntsville, the fastest-growing city in the state, appears to have turned blue. Jones pulled 43% of the vote in Shelby County, a once unthinkable result in what should be a solid GOP area.
That’s not a win. It’s growth, something Democrats have needed for years. Political environments rarely change in a single election cycle. Coalitions are built with time, fresh ideas and realignments over new issues. 
Alabama Democrats have spent the past 16 years struggling to hold what they have. Now they have opportunity. Turning that into victory will require candidate recruitment and investment, especially in city council and county commission races, if Tuesday is going to be more than a one-time surge. It will also require resilience in the face of disappointments and electoral setbacks. 
But Doug Jones may have gotten us closer to two-party politics in Alabama. That’s a far better place to be than where Democrats were. 
It will be an important legacy. And a moral victory in the best sense of the phrase. In Czech playwright Václav Havel’s struggles with his nation’s communist party, he once wrote that “a moral victory may later become a de facto victory.” And after decades of seemingly futile struggles, Havel won.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: Is West Virginia the most exploited state?
description: Of all the states in the country, West Virginia is one of, if not, the most exploited states. From resources like labor, coal and the state's natural beauty to less tangible things like class consciousness and worker solidarity, all of these and other things have been stripped down to a state of bareness or nonexistence.
text:
Scene of actual fighting at the Battle of Blair Mountain, showing armed Logan County deputies returning the attack of miners in the dense thickets hundreds of feet in front of them. This photo appeared in the Charleston Gazette on Sept. 10, 1921. (West Virginia State Archives photo)Of all the states in the country, West Virginia is one of, if not, the most exploited states. From resources like labor, coal and the state’s natural beauty to less tangible things like class consciousness and worker solidarity, all of these and other things have been stripped down to a state of bareness or nonexistence. 
Former Sen. Joe Manchin referred to West Virginia as an extraction state, and as sad as it may be, that might be the most honest thing that he has ever said as a politician. I’d guess he was speaking from his experience of having made a living off the exploitation of his fellow statesmen’s labor and health, via his company Enersystems that has a history of workplace violations and polluting local waterways with toxic elements. Once dubbed “one of the wealthiest Senators in Congress, placing 19th” yet hailing from one of the poorest states in the country; this could only happen with rampant unchecked corruption and exploitation. 
Throughout the state’s history, coal had been the primary economic driver of the state. The majority of jobs were coal related, and the coal companies for a time ruled with a near iron fist; having their own towns, stores, housing and currency until they were forced to pay workers in U.S. dollars.
 The massive industry in the states’ early history is where both corporate exploitation and worker solidarity butted heads. The carelessness, neglectful and exploitative nature of coal company owners in regard to their workers’ rights, labor, health and working conditions is largely what sparked an awakening and uprising of worker solidarity and class consciousness. 
In 1921, the Battle of Blair Mountain was the largest armed conflict on U.S. soil aside from the Civil War, a battle between miners and the coal companies during a series of conflicts referred to as the Mine Wars. This was also the largest display of worker solidarity and unity of the time, and to the exploitative coal barons this was seen as a threat to their positions and their futures that would be at risk. The influential, contagious and effective nature of the miners’ passion and solidarity were viewed as such a threat to profits that the Mine Wars were nearly erased from the history books. Through extracting the state’s main economic resource and crushing worker solidarity at the Battle of Blair Mountain, West Virginia would be set on a path, facing decades of exploitation and immiseration. In the Mine Wars museum there is a plaque that states that the mine wars were:
“The absence of the mine wars and other industrial abuses of power in public discourse and classroom curriculum was no mere oversight but, rather, a deliberate cover up by state officials. During the Great Depression, Gov. Homer Adams Holt threatened to thwart New Deal programs in West Virginia unless the Mine Wars were removed from federally funded history books on the state.
As this collection of publications and textbooks demonstrate, the Mine Wars did not make their way into the narrative for over 50 years, while coal companies were continuously praised as beacons of progress and prosperity.
In the drawers below you will find a chronological series of textbooks, each opened to the portion which should have addressed the West Virginia Mine Wars, but did not.”
Part of the reason this was done was to hide the reality that the mining companies went to extremely violent lengths to prevent the unionization of workers, even establishing the West Virginia State Police as a force to quell and fight protests, protestors and eventually miners turned combatants during the duration of the conflict. Another reason I suspect is to hide the fact that the coal barons effectively defanged, and ruined the reputation of the United Mineworkers of America, even further breaking the state’s worker solidarity. 
As someone that took West Virginia history classes, it was surprising but also infuriating to learn that such an important event in our state, and even our nation’s history, was basically glossed over by the time it was taught to me. This choice had huge ramifications and greatly contributes to the current dire state of worker solidarity, union participation, and the lack of class consciousness we have today.
Over 100 years later, West Virginia continues to be exploited by essentially the same perpetrators: corrupt politicians, the ultra-wealthy and corporations. West Virginia has a long history of corrupt politicians that prioritized enriching themselves, their donors or their egos, at the expense of the state’s people, resources and natural beauty.
A clear example of this brazen exploitation is the fact that black lung rates in West Virginia and the rest of Central Appalachia are significantly higher than the national average by 10x. These companies have always had the money and ability to make safety improvements, but time after time they have prioritized profits over people. Even today, the Mountain State is seemingly being sold off to the companies of tech billionaires just for them to level the land, build their data centers, and exploit the land further. The politicians that have the ability to stop or inhibit this from happening are the same ones giving a pass to corporations, with little to no benefit for those living around the centers. All of this has contributed to West Virginia’s near last place national rank when it comes to most categories, like education, happiness, life expectancy and many others. 
One of the most egregious exploitations that has happened to the people of West Virginia was the manufactured opioid epidemic. Robbing folks of their health and money, taking advantage of the injured to turn them into addicts and lifelong consumers. Generations personally affected by this crisis, whether it’s from losing family members, friends or even themselves to the grip of opioid addiction. I often think about the amount of human potential lost to this epidemic. Nearly everyone in this state, if asked would be able to give testimony to the damage this epidemic caused them. Those responsible for unleashing this upon West Virginia, hardly faced any consequence and settled for buying their way out of any sort of real repercussions. These opioid settlement funds, ordered to go towards programs that reduce opioid and drug use primarily went into the coffers of the police departments and to buy flock cameras. Absolutely shameful
In order for West Virginia to begin toward a positive trajectory, the state needs working class leaders and politicians that are free of outside influence, willing to stand up to corporations and advocate on behalf of the people they serve. Removing money’s influence in elections starting at the local level to ensure a candidate’s accountability to the people. Ending the commodification of life’s essentials such as food, water, shelter, medicine and education would greatly benefit the people of the state, and work to address the many insecurities people here face. 
There needs to be a drastic reassessment of what our priorities are here in the state, as well as, what our government is supposed to be doing and providing for us; perhaps something like fixing a water crisis still ongoing in the southern part of the state? The function of government should be improving material conditions for all its people, instead of the exploitation and immiseration we’ve continued to experience for decades.

title: KY oil well operator fined, sentenced for water pollution
description: A Kentucky oil well operator has been fined $20,000 after admitting he illegally discharged polluted water into a creek in northeast Kentucky. The judge also sentenced Joshua Ferguson, of Martha, to serve 12 months on home detention. The Kentucky Department of Environmental Protection received a tip last fall about brine water from an oil-well site […]
text:
An oil pumpjack casts a shadow on a wall as it pulls oil from the Permian Basin oil field on March 14, 2022 in Odessa, Texas. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)A Kentucky oil well operator has been fined $20,000 after admitting he illegally discharged polluted water into a creek in northeast Kentucky.
The judge also sentenced Joshua Ferguson, of Martha, to serve 12 months on home detention.
The Kentucky Department of Environmental Protection received a tip last fall about brine water from an oil-well site being dumped into a creek known as Left Fork Blaine Creek, which is Lawrence County and ultimately feeds into Yatesville Lake.
Brine water, also called produced water, is a byproduct of oil production.
It can be saltier than seawater and can contain toxic water and radioactive substances, according to a government memorandum in Ferguson’s case.
On Sept. 3, 2025, an inspector found a hose from a brine tank at the site of two oil wells in Lawrence County that led to the creek.
The hose had been buried, but the inspector tracked it and found it was discharging into Left Fork Blaine Creek, according to a plea agreement Ferguson signed.
The water downstream from the discharge was orange and there was no sign of life in the creek.
The inspector talked to Ferguson the next day and he admitted running the hose to the creek to discharge the polluted water.
Ferguson said he had buried the line two years earlier in order to save money on legal disposal costs, according to the court record.
Ferguson, 42, faced up to three years in federal prison for violations of the federal Clean Water Act.
The prosecutor, Assistant U.S. Attorney Emily Greenfield, sought prison time for Ferguson, arguing his offense was serious and continued for an extended period.
“People and companies in this industry must be deterred from polluting to make a profit,” Greenfield said in a sentencing memorandum, referring to the oil and gas industry.
However, Ferguson’s attorney, Stephen W. Owens of Pikeville, said it wasn’t necessary to put Ferguson behind bars.
Owens said Ferguson has worked steadily all his adult life and is well-respected in the community. The federal charge itself was punishment for him, Owens said.
Chief U.S. District Judge David L. Bunning followed the government’s recommendation for a fine of at least $20,000, but did not opt for prison time.
Instead, he placed Ferguson on probation for five years with a year of that on home detention.
Ferguson can leave home for work, church, medical appointments and other approved activities.
Bunning sentenced Ferguson Oct. 13 in federal court in Ashland.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Investment groups challenge Kentucky law aimed at ‘ideological’ investing
description: Investor groups are challenging a Kentucky law they argue would make it harder for shareholders to push companies to consider climate change, diversity and other issues in their policies. The plaintiffs claim the law is unconstitutional, in part because it impairs their right to speak freely under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The […]
text:
Kentucky State Capitol in 2020 before construction project (Photo by Sarah Ladd)Investor groups are challenging a Kentucky law they argue would make it harder for shareholders to push companies to consider climate change, diversity and other issues in their policies.
The plaintiffs claim the law is unconstitutional, in part because it impairs their right to speak freely under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
The law at issue is Senate Bill 183, which was approved in the 2026 session and deals with proxy advisors.
Publicly-traded companies have boards that set policy, but shareholders – who own a piece of the business – can make proposals on how a company should be run.
That can be a mechanism for submitting proposals at odds with, or in addition to, policies a company board and managers have set.
Examples could include submitting proposals for a company to move away from the use of fossil fuels such as coal, or efforts to get companies to incorporate diversity, equity and inclusion measures in their policies.
Proxy advisors provide research and guidance to blocks of investors on voting on such proposals.
SB 183 says a proxy advisory service is “not solely in the interest of shareholders” if it is based on, or takes into account, non-financial factors such as “an environmental, social, political, or ideological interest” not directly connected to the risk or return on an investment.
The law also says a service is not solely in the interest of shareholders if it recommends a proposal at odds with a recommendation from the company board and does not provide a complex economic analysis of the proposal.
The law also requires proxy advisors to notify all shareholders that the proposal was not being provided solely in their interest and that the advice put other objectives ahead of their financial interest, “including sacrificing investment returns or undertaking additional investment risk” to promote non-financial interests such as diversity or environmental concerns.
Proxy advisors could be penalized under the state’s consumer-protection law for violations.
SB 183 passed the Senate 32 to 6 and the House 81 to 6.
Supporters argue the law is aimed at making sure company shareholders have adequate information when voting on proposals.
“It’s about transparency for proxy advisory firms that influence billions of dollars in shareholder votes, including decisions that affect Kentucky pensions and retirement savings,” state Sen Matt Nunn, R-Sadieville, said in a news release in March 2026. “All it says is if you’re giving advice that moves that kind of money, folks deserve to know whether it’s based on financial facts or something else.”
Nunn said there are many non-profits set up “specifically to avoid accountability while pushing ideological agendas” such as diversity, equity and inclusion through corporate decision-making.
“Kentuckians work too hard to have their retirement investments influenced without accountability,” Nunn said in the release.
Nunn and Republican Sens. Robby Mills of Henderson and Steve Rawlings of Burlington sponsored the bill.
Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, vetoed the bill, saying it was unconstitutional because it would expose faith-based investors to extra disclosure and costly litigation and “infringe on their right to exercise their faith in engaging with companies.”
Republican supermajorities in the House and Senate easily overrode Beshear’s veto.
Three organizations filed a lawsuit in federal court Oct. 29 seeking to strike down the law.
The plaintiffs are the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility (ICCR) and United Church Funds, both based in New York, and Ceres, a non-profit based in Boston.
ICCR says it has more than 300 institutional investors as members, more than half of them faith-based but also including asset-management companies, pension funds and others.
They use their shares in companies to call for improved environmental and social concerns, including through shareholder proposals, the coalition says.
United Church Funds, which says it provides investment services to more than 1,000 churches and faith-based organizations, files shareholder resolutions at companies in which members invest, while Ceres works with investors to push measures that include reducing fossil-fuel emissions.
They argue in the lawsuit that SB 183 violates their First Amendment rights in a number of ways.
For example, the law discriminates against the point of view of shareholders who file a proposal that doesn’t agree with the position of a company board, always favoring the company’s position, the complaint argues.
The requirement to provide an economic analysis of shareholder proposals, even though the company board would not have to provide a similar analysis of its proposals, is onerous and discriminatory, according to the lawsuit.
Further, the provision for proxy advisors to notify shareholders that a proposal was not solely in their interest would force the advisors to say something they don’t believe, the complaint says.
“Each Plaintiff’s view about financially prudent investing accounts for interests Kentucky likely construes as ‘political’ or ‘ideological,’ including environmental, social, and governance interests,” the lawsuit says. “In Plaintiffs’ view, all these interests are intimately connected to long-term financial performance.”
The law puts the state’s weight behind corporate leadership and suppresses speech from others, the lawsuit claims.
The legislature “expressly intended both to make it harder for shareholders to speak up against corporate leadership’s positions and to suppress shareholder requests that companies consider important issues affecting long-term performance,” according to the lawsuit.
The lawsuit says the state can disagree with the view that risks related to environmental sustainability have financial effects on the bottom line of companies, but isn’t allowed to “regulate Plaintiffs’ speech out of the marketplace or compel Plaintiffs to speak in furtherance of Kentucky’s views about these issues.”
The lawsuit also claims that terms and requirements in the law are so vague that proxy advisory services would have trouble complying.
Attorney General Russell Coleman is the defendant in the lawsuit because his office defends challenges to state law.
In addition to seeking to strike down SB 183, the lawsuit seeks an injunction barring Coleman from enforcing it and an award of attorney fees for lawyers for the three organizations.
Attorneys with Democracy Forward – a progressive legal group that one publication described as the “nerve center of the legal opposition to Trump – filed the lawsuit along with Amy D. Cubbage, an attorney with Tachau Meek in Louisville and former general counsel to Beshear.
Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, said in a statement that shareholders have a right to challenge corporate leadership and make investment decisions based on their values and understanding of financial risks.
“Attorney General Russell Coleman cannot use the power of the state to silence viewpoints it disagrees with or force organizations to disavow their own beliefs,” Perryman said.
Nunn responded to the lawsuit in a statement issued Monday, saying the law “requires transparency and accountability on the part of proxy advisors doing business in Kentucky in order to protect our Kentucky investors from unfair, false, misleading or deceptive trade practices.”
“I trust that Attorney General Coleman will protect the interests of our Kentucky investors and vigorously defend the constitutionality of Senate Bill 183, which passed by wide margins in both the House and the Senate,” Nunn said.
Coleman’s office did not respond to a request for comment last week.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky sees a ‘slowdown’ of rate of homelessness, but not in all parts of the state
description: The increasing rate of homelessness across Kentucky has slowed down compared to past years, but there are “still too many” people experiencing homelessness.  That’s according to new statewide survey data provided to the Kentucky Lantern this month by the Kentucky Housing Corporation, a quasi-governmental agency that manages federal and state housing funding.[...]
text:
A tent where a homeless person lived is seen in a snowy camp on Dec. 23, 2022 in Louisville. (Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images)The increasing rate of homelessness across Kentucky has slowed down compared to past years, but there are “still too many” people experiencing homelessness. 
That’s according to new statewide survey data provided to the Kentucky Lantern this month by the Kentucky Housing Corporation, a quasi-governmental agency that manages federal and state housing funding. 
The data is from Kentucky’s version of the nationwide Point-in-Time Count where volunteers and agency outreach workers around the beginning of each year seek to count the number of people who lack “a fixed, regular, and adequate nighttime residence,” the federal definition of homeless used for the survey. 
This year’s survey, conducted in February, found that 5,734 people across all 120 counties met that definition across the state, a slight decrease from 2025 when the survey counted 5,789 people experiencing homelessness. Those total numbers encompass people who are unsheltered, in an emergency shelter and in transitional housing.
But the trendlines of homelessness in Kentucky are different depending on the part of the state. 

In Louisville, the survey found a 12% decrease year over year in the total number of people counted, from 1831 to 1609 people. But Lexington and the 118 counties beyond the state’s two largest cities, known as the “Balance of State”, each saw increases in their respective counts of more than 4%. 
Shaye Rabold, a technical administrator for the Kentucky House Corporation, told the Lantern the data shows a “slowdown” in the rate of homelessness after previous years of more dramatic increases. 
She said Louisville has made notable local investments in what’s known as permanent supportive housing, where someone is provided with permanent housing while also receiving other support including financial assistance with utility bills and childcare, substance abuse treatment and other forms of help. But she said that’s generally not the case in other counties.
“The reality is the resources in most of our counties are not enough,” Rabold said, mentioning that many counties lack emergency shelters. “There’s just simply not enough existing affordable housing for people to identify on their own.” 
Rabold said the lack of affordable housing remains the driving reason behind increasing rates of homelessness, though other individual factors including mental health and substance abuse disorders can play a role. A Kentucky Housing Corporation executive said earlier this year that Kentucky is still not building nearly enough housing, particularly for low-income people, to bridge the state’s housing shortage. 
Adrienne Bush, the executive director of the advocacy group Homeless and Housing Coalition of Kentucky, told the Lantern that Trump administration efforts, currently entangled in litigation, to move federal funding away from permanent supportive housing programs has had a “huge impact” and created uncertainty for Kentucky organizations addressing homelessness.  
“I just can’t emphasize enough how that disruption really ultimately impacts the people who are currently experiencing homelessness and who are seeking services,” Bush said. 
Bush said she wouldn’t be surprised if next year’s survey numbers show an increase because organizations in Kentucky aren’t able to fully deploy federal funding because of the uncertainty.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Voters are revolting over affordability. Here’s how to KY officials should respond.
description: For the second election in a row, voters made it clear that affordability is their chief concern. The inflation numbers show us why.  Because of price hikes over the past two years, the median Kentucky household is now spending $4,127 more annually for the same goods and services than they were at the end of […]
text:
Families face higher costs for rent, gas, health care, child care and other essentials. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)For the second election in a row, voters made it clear that affordability is their chief concern. The inflation numbers show us why.  Because of price hikes over the past two years, the median Kentucky household is now spending $4,127 more annually for the same goods and services than they were at the end of 2024.   
Gas prices make up the single biggest item in that increase, but families are also shelling out more for everyday household purchases, utilities, groceries and more. That would matter less if wages were keeping up. But they are not.
An end to the war in Iran and the president’s chaotic, across-the-board tariffs would surely help. But the cost of living was voters’ top priority even before those problems.  
With the Kentucky General Assembly coming up, there are countless ways the state legislature could ease household budget strains. We at the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy laid out dozens of ideas in a comprehensive report last year.
But it makes sense to start with low-hanging fruit, including issues many in the Republican majority already support.
In the 2026 session, lawmakers nearly passed Senate Bill 9, legislation that at least begins to address the housing crisis by streamlining some regulations, encouraging density and allowing a way to clear eviction records. It stalled only because of a last-minute poison pill that would prevent local regulations of short-term rental properties like AirBnBs.
Lawmakers should discard that harmful portion and pass a stronger package. Funding for housing is critical, so the legislature needs to enact HB 411 sponsored by Rep. Steve Bratcher (R-Hardin), which modernizes the real estate fees used to fund the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. And they should take an additional step to jumpstart that fund with one-time dollars. 
A rare, one-time corporate income tax payment this summer has given the state $330 million in unexpected tax revenue. That money could be invested in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund to spur the construction of new mixed-income housing. Legislators have spent nearly $5 billion on capital projects over the last couple of budgets, but only 0.3% of it for housing. Shouldn’t we do more for the biggest cost in any Kentucky family’s budget?
The cost of health care is also a grave concern. The most pressing issue is the need to fully fund Medicaid, which covers one in three Kentuckians and is short $421 million that was left out of the original budget. Otherwise, we’ll see cuts to services, as nearly happened last summer, leading to lost coverage and care and higher costs for everyone seeking health care. The money to make the program whole sits in the Budget Reserve Trust Fund, but lawmakers must appropriate the funds. 
In addition, utility bills continue to strain Kentucky families. The biggest fear in the short term is that the demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers will drive those costs higher. Lawmakers should quickly pass robust rules that prevent Big Tech from passing burdens to ratepayers, require local community involvement and democratic buy-in to the location of data centers, and roll back the enormous tax breaks that the legislature offered these companies. 
Much more can and should be done. From infant care to retirement, from home insurance to health insurance, and from college debt to drug costs — there are commonsense policy actions the state could take to make life more affordable. That includes taking on new forms of price gouging — like the “surveillance pricing” big corporations now use to adjust what you pay in real time based on the data they collect about you.
And let’s not forget the central need to raise wages and job quality for Kentucky workers. Affordability is not just about how much things cost, but how much is in your pocket to pay for them. Very popular ideas to raise wages are already available, like repealing right-to-work, restoring the prevailing wage law, permitting more public sector union organizing, and raising the outdated minimum wage. 
Some of these issues aren’t politically viable yet. But in the 2024 and 2026 elections, voters revolted against incumbents from both parties over the problem of affordability. It’s a risky bet to expect they won’t do so again.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. could lose representation, funding under proposed census rule change, AG Jones, housing orgs say
description: The U.S. Census Bureau has proposed a rule change that would alter aspects of how census data is collected every decade. The adjustments would change who gets counted, where, and what questions are asked.  The changes could affect political representation — like how congressional and state legislative districts are apportioned — as well as how […]
text:
(Photo illustration by States Newsroom)The U.S. Census Bureau has proposed a rule change that would alter aspects of how census data is collected every decade. The adjustments would change who gets counted, where, and what questions are asked. 
The changes could affect political representation — like how congressional and state legislative districts are apportioned — as well as how much state or federal funding communities can get for public services. 
The changes include a shift from counting everybody living in communities to only counting American citizens and lawful permanent residents, changing what counts as a person’s “usual residence,” and ending the collection of information on people’s race and ethnicity. It would also make other demographic questions optional. 
Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said that President Donald Trump’s administration “will stop at nothing to undermine and chip away at our democracy, and their recent effort to attack the census process is the latest example.” 
He added: “Census data determines congressional seats. Census data informs the policy and programs that serve communities. This isn’t a tweak to the way a census is run – it’s Trump’s effort to rig the board, and my office will not stand for it.” 
On Nov. 4, Jones announced Virginia had joined a multi-state challenge to the proposed rule change submitted to the U.S. Department of Commerce. Jones is among over 20 attorneys general from states and Washington, D.C., along with governors from Kentucky and Pennsylvania. 
Housing Opportunities Made Equal of Virginia — a fair housing organization in the state that takes on housing discrimination cases — submitted a letter to U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnik last week in opposition to the changes.
Accurate census information is critical to the work that HOME of Virginia does, policy director Laura Dobbs said in a recent call with The Mercury. 
Housing and legal aid groups in Virginia and other states joined HOME of Virginia in the letter to the secretary. Those include Washington, D.C.-based Equal Rights Center, the Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, the Fair Housing Center of Southwest Michigan, the Legal Aid Justice Center and the Virginia Poverty Law Center. 
“Without this information, it will be harder for fair housing and legal aid organizations like ours to identify and redress longstanding racial, social and other disparities to meet the needs of underserved communities,” the groups stated. 
They requested the secretary have the Bureau withdraw the proposed adjustments entirely. 
“These sweeping changes …  will lead to a decade-long theft of critical funding for food, housing, schools, healthcare, and legal services for our communities,” the organizations added. 
When federal agencies suggest altering how certain functions are carried out, proposals are posted to the Federal Register website for an official public comment period. 
For the proposed census rule, nearly 150,000 responses were submitted to the website between Sep. 10 and Nov. 2, when the comment period closed. 
Beyond leading to funding and political representation changes, Dobbs explained that the new usual residence criteria will create confusion and inaccuracies. 
“(The federal government) would be looking at a newly defined enumeration period that runs from January 1 to April 1 of that year, which I’m sure you can understand would create a lot of confusion,” she said. “They also want to verify that through things like tax records, which aren’t necessarily always showing people’s current residence, so this creates a lot of problems.”
Now that public comment has closed on the proposal, the Trump administration could withdraw their changes, make further adjustments or proceed in the next regulatory steps before the rule could take effect.  
If the administration tries to advance the rule shift, state attorneys general could launch an official legal challenge..
Data collection for the next census is not set until 2030.

title: Virginia localities rethink use of license plate readers amid privacy concerns, report states
description: Seventeen Virginia localities using automatic license plate readers to identify vehicles and investigate crimes are reconsidering or scaling back ALPR use, vendor relationships, or camera installations, a new report found.  The reconsideration comes as local governments and law enforcement agencies face public scrutiny after alleged misuse and disagreements [...]
text:
A view of an automated license plate reader. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Seventeen Virginia localities using automatic license plate readers to identify vehicles and investigate crimes are reconsidering or scaling back ALPR use, vendor relationships, or camera installations, a new report found. 
The reconsideration comes as local governments and law enforcement agencies face public scrutiny after alleged misuse and disagreements over how authorities use the readers.
Nearly all of Virginia’s law enforcement agencies with license plate readers responded to a statewide survey, up from 70% last year. 
But the responses give only a limited picture as agencies reassess their use of the devices, leaving Virginia Crime Commission staff unable to determine whether agencies fully comply with every statutory provision.
Still, speakers at Thursday’s commission meeting argued there may be some noncompliance.
“Dozens of agencies across Virginia (are) breaking the law, with only two people being charged,” said Duane Barron, a board member for Justice Forward, criticizing the report for not assessing whether ALPRs actually make Virginia safer or reflect public views.
 Report results

Last year, staff found several areas of non-compliance that raised concerns regarding agency policies, data retention and data sharing. 
This year’s survey found fewer agencies reporting non-compliance in these areas, including six agencies reporting no policy, down from 26.
Fewer agencies also reported data retention periods over 21 days, down from 33 to seven, and fewer reported continuously sharing ALPR system data with other state law enforcement agencies, down from 20 to four.
The few agencies sharing camera data said it was done to assist with terrorist attacks or threats, at the request of a federal agency for case assistance, a murder investigation and criminal investigations.
Under state law, law-enforcement agencies may share data obtained through ALPR systems under certain circumstances. The statute prohibits sharing or disseminating the data to “any database of any other state, federal, private, or commercial entity.” 
The statute does not, however, expressly prohibit sharing or disseminating the data directly to out-of-state or federal law-enforcement officers.
Staff said only two criminal charges have been filed for unauthorized use, despite approximately 20 reported incidents.
Commission members questioned why the other reported incidents had not resulted in charges and argued that existing consequences might not deter violations, underscoring the policy stakes.
Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, proposed decertifying officers who violate ALPR policy and called for stronger consequences for agencies that fail to follow it.
Other members questioned whether enforcement should be non-discretionary and proposed limiting ALPR access to designated or certified personnel as another safeguard to improve compliance.
House Majority Leader Del. Charniele Herring, D-Alexandria, said members could consider the policy ideas at the next meeting on Tuesday.
Last year, Herring carried the commission’s recommendation, which led to successful legislation allowing the use of license plate reader systems, like those operated by Flock.
The new law establishes statewide approval, restricts police use of ALPR technology, requires documentation and reporting, and creates oversight to monitor use and accountability.
“My primary concern … was to ensure that we were using technology in a responsible manner that balances people’s right to privacy and their safety,” Herring said.
 Public reacts to report

No public-testimony speaker clearly advocated for keeping ALPRs in use; most speakers called for a statewide ban on the readers, including Flock — most commonly used by agencies — Axon and Motorola. 
However, some acknowledged limited potential benefits, including Barron, who said ALPRs might help locate a stolen car or lost scooter, but argued that wasn’t the central question.
Tamara Lewis, a National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers representative, argued that the technology could help identify stolen vehicles or respond to Amber Alerts, while pushing for warrants and much shorter data retention.
“These are no longer tools that merely identify license plates. These are mass surveillance networks that record the travels of everyone with the vehicle,” Lewis said.
Hampton Commonwealth’s Attorney Anton Bell, who sits on the commission, said his colleagues have seen “great benefits” from license plate readers in response to the report.
“However, with any law enforcement tool, we recognize there has to be always be checks and balances on anything where there’s the availability or opportunity for abuse,” Bell said.
 What’s next

Lawmakers will return to Richmond for the next General Assembly session in January to discuss related legislation. Some lawmakers have publicly expressed interest in banning the readers, while others have called for more transparency and stronger oversight.
Del. Jackie Glass, D-Norfolk, carried two proposals last session that would have established statewide oversight, operating standards and training requirements for ALPRs. The bills were continued to January.
No related legislation had been filed as of Friday afternoon.
The commission will hold its final meeting before the next session on Tuesday. The agenda has not been set.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: After the blue tsunami, Democrats in Va., nationwide should avoid misinterpreting their mandate
description: After a win as sweeping as Tuesday was for the Democratic Party nationally, Democrats representing Virginia and other states might imagine they hold an unlimited mandate for anything and everything they want to prioritize once they take control of Congress in January. It would likely be their swift undoing, as history affirms. In the enthusiasm […]
text:
Voters receive an "I voted" sticker in Spotsylvania County on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)After a win as sweeping as Tuesday was for the Democratic Party nationally, Democrats representing Virginia and other states might imagine they hold an unlimited mandate for anything and everything they want to prioritize once they take control of Congress in January.
It would likely be their swift undoing, as history affirms.
In the enthusiasm wave elections like this generate, victors find it irresistible not to presume that voters emphatically validated all of their ideas. They did not.
It is clear from Tuesday’s exit polls conducted by NBC News and other media groups that this was not so much a vote for Democrats as it was a referendum against a deeply disliked Republican president and a GOP Congress that failed to protect the public from his capricious, harmful actions.
The cost of living was by far the most pressing issue on voters’ minds this election, and they held the GOP responsible, but the polling also shows that there was no majority for either party when voters were asked which is best prepared to fix it.
Two of every three voters surveyed said Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions. Almost the same share disapproved of the way Trump is handling the presidency, and 77% disapproved of Congress’s performance.
But when asked their opinion about the Democratic Party, 52% voiced an unfavorable view of it while 60% disfavored the GOP.
Warner wins fourth term, Luria ousts Kiggans in VA-02, Taylor triumphs in VA-01

Virginia was part of the blue wave, but its results were unremarkable compared to epic upsets in House and Senate races. Democrats flipped two Republican-held Virginia seats that polling showed were vulnerable.
Democrat Shannon Taylor edged 10-term Republican incumbent Rob Wittman in the 1st District and Democrat Elaine Luria won back the seat Republican Jen Kiggans took from her in the 2022 midterm in Virginia’s 2nd District. Virginia’s House delegation will have an 8-3 Democratic majority in the next Congress.
A third House race was close but, as expected, the seat remained in GOP hands. Democratic former Rep. Tom Perriello came just short in his bid to reclaim from Republican Rep. John McGuire the 5th District seat he won in a 2008 Democratic wave and held for one term.
Democratic incumbent Sen. Mark Warner easily brushed aside Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa in what the former governor says is his fourth and final Senate campaign. The outcome was never in doubt.
The headlines went to states such as Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and even Mississippi that had been solidly red since the 20th century, until Democrats either unseated Republicans or held unlikely leads when Tuesday’s counts were finished.
We’ve seen wave elections like this before. 
This was the fifth time since World War II that American voters in midterms have shifted control of both chambers of Congress from one party to the other. In 1946 and 1994, Republicans swept Democrats out of power during Democratic presidencies. Democrats ousted the GOP in 1954, 2006 and again this week.
Twenty years ago, Republican President George W. Bush squandered the popularity he held after the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks from the misbegotten Iraq invasion and widespread dissatisfaction with a GOP Congress. Voters punished Republicans at the midpoint of Bush’s second term.
In 1994, voters ended decades of Democratic congressional dominance midway through Democratic President Bill Clinton’s first term. History largely credits Rep. Newt Gingrich, R-Ga., a younger and more confrontational field of GOP candidates and their “Contract With America,” but voters were actually fatigued with Democrats and what they saw as overreach under Clinton.
Exit polls from that election showed that a majority of voters knew nothing about the “Contract With America.” Only a small percentage could identify any item within it, and those who knew the most were the most opposed to the Republican candidates.
Backlashes like those that precipitated these midterm house-cleanings may become more common as the electorate becomes more culturally divided and politically volatile. We are in a pattern of voter discontent and anger at whomever happens to be in control.
Democrats already have signaled their intention to hold investigations of claims of Trump administration corruption. That is properly Congress’s role. But there is a danger that voters will view it as more partisan retribution done at the expense of addressing problems like the cost of living that they were elected to solve. That’s how backlashes can turn into wave elections.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania’s Democratic trifecta renews calls to join National Popular Vote compact
description: Already enacted in 18 states and the District of Columbia, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would bypass the Electoral College to guarantee the candidate with the most votes across the country wins the presidency.
text:
Already enacted in 18 states and the District of Columbia, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would bypass the Electoral College to guarantee the candidate with the most votes across the country wins the presidency. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Democrats’ midterm victories in Pennsylvania and other swing states have prompted renewed interest in an alternative to the Electoral College that proponents have urged the commonwealth to join.
With Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro’s reelection and majorities in both chambers of the General Assembly, Democrats have a clear runway to launch popular progressive initiatives, such as increasing the minimum wage and protecting abortion rights under state law. 
The commonwealth’s blue trifecta would also make it easier for lawmakers to pass legislation that supporters say would ensure that every vote counts in presidential elections.
Already enacted in 18 states and the District of Columbia, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would guarantee the candidate with the most votes across the country wins the presidency. Pennsylvania’s neighboring states Delaware, New Jersey and New York are among the members of the compact. 
“Every voter in Pennsylvania should matter in every presidential election, not just when it’s so tight a court has to decide who won it,” said Patrick Rosenstiel, senior consultant to National Popular Vote. “We want voters in every state to participate and be involved in the presidential election.”
Five presidential elections have been won via the Electoral College by candidates who lost the popular vote. They include President George W. Bush who became president after the 2000 election despite losing to Vice President Al Gore by more than half a percentage point and President Donald Trump, who lost the popular vote to former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by about a half point.
Rosenstiel added that he’s increasingly confident that a favorable environment with political support and legislative will exists to advance the legislation here. As a lifelong Republican and a resident of blue Minnesota, he added that the compact should appeal to any voter who feels their presidential vote hasn’t mattered.
While Rosenstiel said the concept is favored by 63% of Americans, others say its passage would foment voter backlash.
“It’s an exceedingly undemocratic idea,” Duquesne University constitutional law professor Bruce Ledewitz said, noting that he’s not opposed to a national popular vote to choose the president but doesn’t support the compact.
“You have to think about what it’s going to be like at the time,” he said, offering a hypothetical scenario. “The people will have voted for Trump, and suddenly the electors are voting for Biden … We already have distrust of the government; that would be a disaster.”

State Sen. Maria Colette (D-Montgomery) said flipping control of the Senate to a Democratic majority gives lawmakers “a real chance” to advance bipartisan election bills that languished in committees for years. “The National Popular Vote Compact is part of that conversation,” she said.
Shapiro said in an interview Saturday with “Pod Save America” host Jon Favreau at a Washington, D.C., event that he’s open to the idea of a national popular vote.
“I’ll work with lawmakers to figure out what the right mechanism is for moving forward on that. But look, we’re the ultimate swing state in Pennsylvania … I think Pennsylvania can still play a massive role even in a national popular vote,” Shapiro said.

Shapiro:  I think the national popular vote makes sense…I'll work with lawmakers to figure out what the right mechanism is for moving forward on that. But look, we're the ultimate swing state in Pennsylvania…I think Pennsylvania can still play a massive role even in a… pic.twitter.com/1ZW2TPpSYw
— Pod Save America (@PodSaveAmerica) November 7, 2026

So, what is the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact and what would Pennsylvania lawmakers need to do to join it?
An interstate compact is a legally binding agreement in which two or more states pass laws in concert with each other to further a common goal. They’re often used to create government agencies that work across state lines to oversee ports, such as the Delaware River Port Authority, or watersheds, like the Susquehanna River Basin Commission. Compacts also exist to ensure credentials including medical licenses are recognized across state lines.  
Under the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, states pass legislation to commit their Electoral College votes to the candidate who receives the most votes out of all 50 states. 
The states that have joined since 2007 collectively have 222 of the 270 Electoral College votes needed to win the presidency. That leaves 48 needed before the compact would take effect, Rosenstiel said.
With 19 Electoral College votes, Pennsylvania is one of the battleground states with state government trifectas National Popular Vote is now targeting along with Michigan (15 votes), Wisconsin (10), Arizona (11) and Nevada (6).
“We want every state who wants their voters to permanently matter in presidential elections,” Rosenstiel said, noting the commonwealth has been both a battleground and a flyover state. “What a national popular vote for president will do is lock in your permanent battleground state status because you’re not guaranteed that.”
Pennsylvania state lawmakers have pushed for the commonwealth to join since at least 2022. 
That’s when Rep. Chris Rabb (D-Philadelphia) introduced legislation backed by eight Democratic co-prime sponsors to join the compact. 
“We need to ensure that the voice of the people is heard, and that no election official can bow to public pressure to change the results of an election,” Rabb, who was elected to Congress last week, said at the time.
His proposal came after the 2020 election when 19 Pennsylvania Republicans submitted their names as alternate electors, voting for Trump when President Joe Biden won the commonwealth’s popular vote.
“We must defer to the collective will of voters irrespective of the victor’s party affiliation and uphold our constitutional imperative with rigor and integrity,” Rabb added.
This legislative session, Collett and Sen. Katie Muth, also a Montgomery County Democrat, circulated a memorandum seeking cosponsors for national popular vote legislation but didn’t introduce a bill.
Rep. Heather Boyd (D-Delaware) said she plans to introduce the legislation next session. She noted that she had received calls last week from colleagues whose constituents had asked about the compact. Boyd added that although Democrats will have at least a 111 seat majority in the 203-member House, she hopes for Republican co-sponsors.  
“I do think the bill would be more powerful if it were understood by members to be a bipartisan effort,” she said.
In a statement Friday, Collett indicated she and Muth remain committed to, “ensuring that every vote in Pennsylvania carries the same importance as every vote in Texas and Montana and every single state in our union.”
“Pennsylvanians just told us what they want from their government, and election reform is part of that. People want a system where voting is easy to understand, ballots are counted fairly and on time, and every vote carries the same weight,” Collett said.

title: A look inside how Democrats made big gains in the Indiana Legislature
description: Frustrated by more than a decade of near irrelevance, some Indiana Democratic legislators sensed more than a year ago that they had a breakthrough opportunity with the 2026 midterm election.
text:
Indiana Reps. Ed DeLaney (from left), Cherrish Pryor, Phil GiaQuinta, Carey Hamilton, Vanessa Summers and Greg Porter celebrate during the state Democratic Party election night gathering on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Frustrated by more than a decade of near irrelevance, some Indiana Democratic legislators sensed more than a year ago that they had a breakthrough opportunity with the 2026 midterm election.
Their strategy — more candidate recruitment, better fundraising and strategic spending — paid off as the national Democratic wave helped the party gain 16 Indiana House seats, which included a reelection loss for Republican House Speaker Todd Huston.
Republicans will still hold a 54-46 House majority for the 2027 legislative session — but the Democratic seat flips amount to the most from a single election in more than 50 years.
Here’s at look at how Democrats pulled it off:
Have candidates everywhere
Democrats were on the ballot in 97 of the 100 state House races this year after they fielded no candidates for 26 districts in the 2024 election.
Democratic House Caucus Chair Carey Hamilton said it was a “very intentional” goal to fill as many ballot spots as possible. That intense recruiting began in the spring and summer of 2025.
It involved talks with county party officials, along with local civic leaders, teacher groups and labor unions, the Indianapolis representative said.
“We were reaching out to our networks across the state, and letting them know we were going to be fighting really hard in ’26 and needed great people running,” Hamilton told the Capital Chronicle.
One such candidate was Misti Meehan, who ran against eight-term Republican Rep. Bob Morris of Fort Wayne after he faced no challengers in either the 2022 or 2024 elections.
Democratic Rep. Misti Meehan of Fort Wayne. (Campaign photo)
Despite being a former Allen County Democratic chair, Meehan received no money from state party committees. She unseated Morris with 51% of the vote, even though she had less than $10,000 in campaign cash. Morris had more than $200,000.
“Everybody was, ‘Hey, try to get 45%,’ and I’m like, ‘No, I’m going to try to win,’” she said in an interview.
Meehan said she was motivated to run after “watching all the money get sucked out of public schools” and safety-net programs while Republicans touted the growing state budget surplus.
“I think as these things are coming to fruition and being enacted and the actual effects of some of this are hitting our communities, people don’t like what they’re seeing,” she said. “I think that provoked people to show up.”
Voters also gave Democrats wins in suburban Indianapolis districts that Republicans had held continuously back to the 1970s or longer, according to a database maintained by?for the political history website Capitol & Washington. 
Democrats won in a cluster of north suburban districts — including Huston’s seat — in an area that had become more competitive over the past few election cycles. 
But three little-known Democrats stunned even party leaders by knocking off incumbent Republicans Bob Behning, Julie McGuire and Andrew Ireland in what had been solid Republican districts in southern Marion County.
Those three Democrats combined for less than $20,000 in campaign fundraising and didn’t get any financial boosts from state party sources, according to filings with the Indiana Election Division. 
Mike Murphy, who was a GOP legislator from southern Indianapolis for 16 years until 2010, said the possibility of those seats flipping “wasn’t on anybody’s radar.”
Murphy said many voters were clearly out to repudiate President Donald Trump.
“For whatever reason you want to be mad at Trump, you can’t vote against him this time,” Murphy said. “So what do you do? You take it out on the next Republican down the line.” 
Republicans didn’t run challengers this year against 20 incumbent Democratic House members, including 10 from Indianapolis and five from northwestern Indiana’s Lake County.
Murphy said it was smart for Democrats to be poised with candidates across the state for a wave election in their favor.
“There’s an old saying in politics: you can’t win with nobody,” he said.
Jumping on opportunities
Democrats have languished with little influence in the House since Republicans captured a supermajority with the 2012 election.
 By having more than two-thirds of the House membership, Republicans could have taken action on bills even if the Democratic members weren’t present.
“Breaking the supermajority” was a consistent goal that Democrats had missed in seven straight elections since then, with Republicans holding 70-30 margins after both the 2022 and 2024 elections.
As this year’s election grew near, Democrats saw poll results in the Indianapolis suburb of Fishers that startled them, said Rep. Ed DeLaney of Indianapolis.
“It was just amazing how strong the Democrats were,” DeLaney said.
Dem challenger defeats Indiana House GOP leader in stunning upset

Those numbers for an area making up much of Huston’s district — and word that the Republican speaker was apparently worried enough to do door-to-door canvassing after not having a Democratic opponent in 2024 or 2022 — sparked a decision to go after him.
The House Democratic campaign leadership directed nearly $250,000 in late October for advertising against Huston.
One TV ad labeled Huston as “the man pulling all the strings in Indiana,” criticizing him for the state’s data center policies, gas tax increases and property tax changes blamed for reduced school funding.
Huston lost his bid for an eighth term in the House as Democrat Lauren Cole received 51.5% of the vote.
“This was a conscious attempt. It was not a smart aleck move to force him to waste money,” DeLaney said. “It was an attempt to dethrone him and it worked.”
Huston said in a concession statement that he was “incredibly proud of the progress we’ve made in Indiana to grow our economy, bring good-paying jobs to our state, lower taxes and create thriving communities.”
“This was an incredibly challenging midterm election and ultimately the national headwinds were too difficult to overcome in a number of our races,” he said.
That same polling prompted Democrats to go bigger in a neighboring district where they pumped in some $300,000 in advertising money during October to help Stephanie Jo Yocum defeat GOP Rep. Chris Jeter of Fishers by eight percentage points.
House Democratic Leader Phil GiaQuinta of Fort Wayne said the day after Election Day that he had been surprised by the campaign polling.
“Maybe I shouldn’t have been, because I go door to door myself, and I hear what Hoosiers have to say, and they were very frustrated,” he said.
Better fundraising — and Beau Bayh
The long Republican supermajority established years of campaign fundraising dominance as individuals, business groups and activist organizations were much more generous to the party they felt certain would control the legislative agenda.
House Republicans reported raising about $6.5 million for their main campaign committee through early October for this year’s campaigns.
Democrats, meanwhile, had raised about $2.5 million by Oct. 9. But that figure was about 50% more than the roughly $1.7 million their campaign arm raised for the 2024 campaign.
Republican cash advantage showing up with late spending in Indiana legislative races

Some of that came from convincing Indiana donors to support in-state candidates rather than sending money to states where they thought Democrats had better chances.
Hamilton said House Democrats ultimately had about $3.5 million with the help of national party groups.
“We’ve always believed that we didn’t need to raise as much as them, but we needed to raise enough to get our message out and to make sure voters understood what their choices were,” she said.
The prospect of Beau Bayh leading the Democratic ticket this year as the secretary of state candidate also factored into campaign planning.
That paid off as Bayh defeated Republican Max Engling by nine percentage points for the first statewide Democratic victory since 2012.
“We were prepared to ride a blue wave, but we were also prepared to deal with the benefits that Beau Bayh gave to us,” DeLaney said. “We knew we’d get more attention, more participation, because of his name and his candidacy.”
What it all will mean
House Republicans picked Rep. Ben Smaltz of Auburn last week as their choice to take the speaker’s chair for the legislative session starting in early January.
Despite the much more narrow majority, Smaltz said Republicans were “still going to operate like a body in the majority.”
He also cited the “national headwinds” for the election losses suffered by state and local Republicans.
Indiana House Republicans pick new leader after big election losses

Democrats also gained five seats in the state Senate with last week’s election. Republicans will retain their supermajority with a 35-15 margin.
The 16 House seats gained by Democrats represent the largest single election jump by either party for the chamber since Democrats flipped 28 seats with the post-Watergate scandal election in 1974, according to the Capital & Washington database.
The last previous significant swing in legislative control came with the 2010 election, when Republicans flipped 12 seats to gain a 60-40 majority. They controlled redistricting in that cycle and added nine more seats in the 2012 election to establish the supermajority that lasted through 14 legislative sessions.
House Democrats say that while they are still in the minority, they expect to have more influence over state spending priorities, education policies and other issues than they have had for many years.
“We got hungry,” DeLaney said. “We had people that didn’t want to stay in this position.”
