title: Language can be a barrier to childcare. New report explores what NH can learn from other states.
description: A new report from the Carsey School of Public Policy examines the barriers preventing non-English-speaking childcare providers and families from accessing childcare systems and resources, and what the other 49 states and Washington, D.C., have done to remove those barriers.  The process for figuring out childcare can be complicated. In addition to finding an[...]
text:
A new report from the UNH Carsey School of Public Policy examines what states are doing to address language barriers to childcare access. Here, a reading and play nook at Kids by the Common in Londonderry. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)A new report from the Carsey School of Public Policy examines the barriers preventing non-English-speaking childcare providers and families from accessing childcare systems and resources, and what the other 49 states and Washington, D.C., have done to remove those barriers. 
The process for figuring out childcare can be complicated. In addition to finding an affordable program with capacity, families also have to navigate financial assistance and other government forms and consider care compatibility. 
The brief, “Solutions From Across the United States to Improve Language Access in Child Care Systems,” found that there is an increased communication barrier surrounding childcare infrastructure for non-native English speakers. The report analyzes solutions individual states have taken to promote language access for both families and providers. 
Evan England is assistant director for the Center of Social Policy in Practice within the Carsey School and one of the co-authors of the report. They said language barriers are also an inhibitor to families accessing childcare. 
“It’s really commonplace in New Hampshire that we understand that access to childcare is something that we need to be talking about and that there are some really common barriers that families experience, like cost or availability,” England said. “But if we really want all families to have access, there are other things that are really important too, and language access is one of them.”
The report identified five strategies some states have incorporated into their systems: giving families easy access to resources in different languages from first contact; having system-wide navigation and translation resources; supporting the supply of language-diverse childcare programs; tracking and promoting language access across state systems; and clarity in who is in charge of making it all work. 
In practice, this looks different across every state, and England wrote that not every state is doing all five strategies at the same time. Childcare funding at the federal and state levels gives programs and governments flexibility in how they execute different ideas. 
For example, families in Massachusetts have access to language interpretation from when they are first entering the childcare system. They are provided financial assistance across multiple languages on their websites. 
In Washington state, the government offers a Dual Language Designation program as a way to incentivize them to grow the supply of language-diverse care. Participating providers get access to training, coaching, recognition and funding opportunities to provide multilingual care. 
England said the goal of the research is to determine how practices in other states could be replicated in New Hampshire. 
“New Hampshire is unique in a lot of ways, but that doesn’t mean that there aren’t things that we can learn from other states,” they said. “Every state approaches language access a little bit differently, and so we can all learn from each other. It’s not only about New Hampshire; it’s about all of us learning different strategies.”
The Carsey School is currently working on New Hampshire-related language access research, which is expected to be published in the coming months.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Gov. Evers joins criminal justice advocates at EXPO gala
description: Tamra Oman, the recipient of the Ramiah Whiteside Changemaker Award at the EXPOnentially Correcting the Narrative 2026 gala in the  Madison Concourse Hotel ballroom on Saturday night, recalled her first meeting with Jerome Dillard, the former executive director of Ex-incarcerated People Organization (EXPO) in 2003. They met in a basement with 30 people and r[...]
text:
Gov. Tony Evers listens to EXPO honoree Tamra Oman, a formerly incarcerated person who now works helping people currently incarcerated in Wisconsin prisons. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner) The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Tamra Oman, the recipient of the Ramiah Whiteside Changemaker Award at the EXPOnentially Correcting the Narrative 2026 gala in the  Madison Concourse Hotel ballroom on Saturday night, recalled her first meeting with Jerome Dillard, the former executive director of Ex-incarcerated People Organization (EXPO) in 2003. They met in a basement with 30 people and raised $35 for a group called Voices Beyond Bars.
She contrasted that small start with the large gathering Saturday of criminal justice advocates and those they represent, along with Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers, Wisconsin Secretary of the Department of Corrections Jared Hoy and Evers’s chief legal counsel and chair of the newly created Commutation Advisory Board, Mel Barnes.
“We have formerly incarcerated leaders,” she said of those in attendance. “We have Department of Corrections leaders. We have the governor of the state of Wisconsin. We have family members,” Oman said, adding, “30 people in a room to a 450 count.”
The Saturday event was a collaborative effort between EXPO, an organization of formerly incarcerated people working for a better future for those impacted by incarceration, and The Community, a statewide organization assisting people inside prisons and after their release.
Both EXPO and The Community, each founded in 2014, were celebrating their sixth anniversary, so the two organizations decided to hold a joint event.
“Bringing two organizations together for anything can be difficult, especially something that is much of our identity as an annual celebration,” said Shannon Ross, the executive director and founder of The Community. “We all have our own practices and our own traditions and our own ideas, but if we can’t come together on things that are large and difficult like this, how can we ask the system and ask society for criminal legal system change?”
The event included  a phone tree where attendees could  listen to recorded conversations between people in prison and their family members. There was also artwork by artists who had been incarcerated, and a large display of framed posters of people who had served their time in prison but, after years of supervision and being responsible members of society, were still facing more years of parole or extended supervision. The exhibit questioned supervision over five years.
Ross said crime survivors are not helped in the criminal justice system because it is built to be adversarial and doesn’t lean toward healing but “fear-based mannerisms.”
“Tonight we are going to hear from someone who is very familiar with both sides of the criminal culture,” said Ross, introducing crime survivor  Melissa Ludin. 
“Today I come into this conversation as someone who has caused harm, and someone who has lost a loved one to violence,” said Lundin.
Melissa Lundin spoke about being both an offender  and victim of crime. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
She recounted how at age 19 she attempted suicide because of the grief of losing her father. She drove her car into an intersection and, she said, “caused devastating harm to other people and many families.”
She received a 25-year sentence and said in six months she would finish 20 years of supervision.
“Over those years, I’ve made amends, including with the person I harmed,” she said, “and I’ve worked to become someone that my children can look up to and depend on. Then I found myself on the other side of violence.”
She recounted the death of Chad Wilson, a criminal justice advocate who worked with Lundin and with whom she had a child. He was killed on Dec. 21, 2021, intentionally run over by a woman he had only known for 24 hours.
Lundin recounted how she struggled with wanting the woman to receive justice but also suffer.
“Justice meant she needed to answer for what she had done,” she said. “Vengeance was part of me that wanted her to hurt because we were hurting, and I felt both.”
She recounted speaking at the Wisconsin Resource Center, and knowing that the woman who had killed Wilson was in the audience. She questioned whether she wanted to be there, but then finally asked to shake the hand of every woman in attendance, including Wilson’s killer.
“I don’t know her full story, but people who cause harm can also have been victims themselves, and I know what it is to carry pain without knowing what to do with it,” Lundin said. “Understanding that matters if we want to prevent harm and accountability matters, too.”
Marriane Oleson, co-executive director of Expo, thanked Gov. Evers for bringing back commutations, a reduction or modification of a criminal sentence under the state’s constitutional authority, using his authority to issue executive orders.
“Thank you for the hope of being seen for who a person has become,” she said. “Shannon and I, with others in this room, hear every day from people holding that hope very carefully, people who have spent years understanding the harm they cause, who are preparing to come home. They are trying to imagine where they could belong. We also recognize the people who have been harmed. Their healing deserves support, and every decision about someone’s future carries real responsibility. I know something about rebuilding a life. I began as an EXPO fellow less than two years after coming home from prison, and today I stand here as the co-executive director. It’s given my life purpose.”
Ross noted the special exhibit for those on supervision who are hanging by a thread, and their photo spinning represents the tenuous nature of being associated with anyone who violates their supervision and also being vulnerable to having their freedom revoked and being sent back to prison just on an allegation.
“Many people on paper (supervision) try to stay out of getting involved and participating in a lot of things in the public and civic space because they don’t feel they’ll be given the benefit of the doubt if something happens when we’re trying to just help people,” he said.
The family of Alejandro Silva, an incarcerated man, was given an award for supporting him while he is still incarcerated.
“I’m just, so you know, grateful and thankful and appreciative for everything that they do for me,”  Silva said on a recorded phone call.
Delilah Franklin, wife of Dennis Franklin, the co-executive director of EXPO, and a member of the Silva family, spoke of her admiration for the family.
The Silva Family was honored for their support of family member, Alejandro, who is in prison. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
“When someone is sentenced, their family serves a sentence, too,” she said. “They may not be behind those walls, but they carry the heartache, the worry, the sleepless nights, and the silent pain comes, to see someone they love in prison. And somehow they still have to get up every morning, go to work, take care of their families, and carry on with a life while a piece of their heart is somewhere else. That is exactly what the Silva family does. They travel for visits, sometimes multiple times a week. They make the video calls, answer the phone, include Alejandro in family decisions, and make sure even the youngest nieces and nephews know him, love him, and build memories with him. They refuse to let incarceration erase Alejandro’s place in their family.”
Democrat Evan Goyke (right) and Republican Michael Schraa. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
Former Assembly representatives Michael Schraa (R-Oshkosh) and Milwaukee City Attorney Evan Goyke, who previously served as a Democratic state representative, were honored for their bipartisan efforts to advance criminal justice legislation, including making vocational training part of the state’s earned release program.
Schraa and Goyke both said that, even though they were on opposite political sides, they became friends and found common ground on legislation.
Goyke celebrated the recent wave of midterm election victories by  Democrats, but cautioned that legislation passed without bipartisan support can be repealed. He offered the example of a “package of criminal justice reform bills called justice reinvestment” passed between 2006-10 by a Democratic Legislature and governor, only to be rescinded under the Republican administration of Gov. Scott Walker. 
Marty Dunmore, the founder of the Dunmore Project was honored for creating an organization that collaborates with other groups to promote safety and healing.
Dunmore lost a daughter to cancer in 2019 just before her 18th birthday, and then subsequently two other daughters were injured, one fatally, in an accident caused by a fifth-time drunk driver, and then a year later the daughter who survived the vehicle injury died by gun violence.
Marty Dunmore featured in a video about her experience of losing three daughters and forming the Dunmore Project (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
“And at the end of the day, I am just a mother who has lost three children, two of which were so preventable,” said Dunmore on video. “So we have to go back to the preventive measures, restorative justice, to meeting people, meeting the youth where they are.”
Marian Wasierski of the citizen’s group Enough is Enough, addressing reckless vehicle driving, said Dunmore was an inspiration.
“Marty refuses to remain frozen in the moment of shock to be seen only as that mother broken by cruel death and immobilized by profound grief,” said Wasierski.  “Marty refuses to allow her sorrow to undo her bottom line, her non-negotiable tenet that the goodness of her girls will never be lost or forgotten.”
Dunmore said she had experienced unimaginable grief, and the Dunmore Project was one place to focus her love for her daughters and share it with others, hoping it will make a difference.
Ronald Watson, another honoree, was nominated by Focused Interruption, a volunteer group that addresses gun violence in Dane County.
In his video presentation, Watson recounted his successful efforts to reintegrate into society after leaving prison in 1993, including working in the restaurant industry, making connections in the community, getting married, starting a family, and staying accountable to his support system.
“I just want to continue to do the work and help other people, no matter how small it be,” he said. “I just want to help others,”
Anthony Cooper, CEO and founder of Focused Interruption, said of Watson, “This brother here is a man of integrity. He continues to want to do the right thing for the right reason, and not just sometimes, but all the time. He wants to make sure he continues to honor his family, continues to honor the work that he’s doing, and continues to honor the community that he’s attached to.”
“Tamra has touched thousands of lives,” said Dillard, introducing Oman for her award. “That’s no exaggeration.”
Oman said she had met Ramiah Whiteside, the namesake of her award, while he was still in prison, and he impressed her because he advocated for others, not knowing if he would ever gain his freedom.
Recorded phone calls between those incarcerated and their family member could be heard by picking up a phone at this exibit. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
“When I think about what it means to be a change maker, I don’t think about grand gestures,” she said. “What I think about is someone who refuses to accept the world as it is because it can be better. Yes, a change maker sees the possibilities, but other people see just problems. A change maker sees people for who they are, not what they did, but what they can be. Most of all, change makers believe that every single person has value, and every life has the power to create something meaningful.”
Gov. Evers was the last to be honored for restoring the pardon advisory board and pardoning over 2,400, offering commutations and pursuing criminal justice reforms.
“We’ve also expanded the successful earned release program, and we provided the highest level of funding ever for the state’s treatment and diversion program to help reduce recidivism and get folks the resources they need to use,” said Evers. “We also expanded the popular Windows to Work program, enabling more folks to participate in programming that increases general work skills, financial literacy, and work search abilities that will help them to be successful after they’re released.”
He noted the recent opening of the Type One Southeast Regional Care System for Youth in Milwaukee, which he said, “represents nearly a decade of work to transform a failed juvenile correction system.”
He added, “last year I introduced a corrections reform plan to modernize our deteriorating prisons, stabilize our population, and expand evidence-based programming to improve public safety and efficiency in the system. This includes expanding community-based options for alternatives to revocation. As well as providing meaningful supports for those facing housing instability, substance use recovery, reentry programs, and more.”
“Unfortunately, Republicans have rejected these common-sense proposals without offering any comprehensive alternatives of their own; my plan is still the safest, fastest, and cheapest option to overhaul the state’s dated correctional system. Every day of delay or inaction makes projects costlier and the goalposts that much harder to reach.”
He encouraged the audience to keep pressure on state leaders to pursue reforms that “keep our communities safe while giving folks the second chance that they deserve.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Kansas Democrats rollicked and reveled after shocking election results. But they weren’t a surprise.
description: Last week’s midterm election was unprecedented but predictable, jaw-dropping but routine, earth-shattering but rock solid. For the first half of those comparisons, you just have to look at the numbers. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since 1932. For the first time in its entire history as a state, Kansas voters picked a Democrat to […]
text:
Jade Piros de Carvalho, right, and Julie Lorenz celebrate as other Kansas Democrats win their races while the governor election remains undetermined at Democrat Cindy Holscher's watch party Nov. 3, 2026, in Lenexa. (Photo by Baya Burgess for Kansas Reflector)
Last week’s midterm election was unprecedented but predictable, jaw-dropping but routine, earth-shattering but rock solid.
For the first half of those comparisons, you just have to look at the numbers. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since 1932. For the first time in its entire history as a state, Kansas voters picked a Democrat to to succeed a Democratic governor (apparently). Kansas elected a Democratic attorney general, kicking square-jawed gadfly Kris Kobach to the curb. And it elected a stunning 20 additional Democrats to the Kansas House.

             
Sunflower State Democrats haven’t seen results like this in the modern era.
On the other hand — and this is where I find myself repeatedly focused last week — what happened on Tuesday was exactly what one might have expected to happen when the nation’s president has an approval rating in the 30s. It’s what one might have expected with sky-high fuel prices, inflation still hot, and the nation embroiled in a foreign war of choice.
For the past decade and change, Republicans and Democrats have deluded themselves into believing that the law of political gravity wouldn’t apply to their parties.
Under President Barack Obama, Democrats hoped that overhauling the nation’s healthcare system would come without electoral costs — they lost 63 seats in the U.S. House. Under President Donald Trump, Republicans prayed that their 2024 coalition wold survive the antics of a would-be authoritarian obsessed with interior decorating, pardoning criminals and muscular hindquarters. The almighty ignored their pleas.
The laws of politics can be suspended for an election or two, given unexpected events. See Republicans under President George W. Bush after the Sept. 11 attacks, or Democrats under President Bill Clinton after his impeachment. But gravity persists.
 
Cindy Holscher, the Democratic candidate for Kansas governor, closes her Nov. 3, 2026, election watch party in Lenexa with a hopeful speech before the close race can be called. (Photo by Baya Burgess for Kansas Reflector)
Democratic swing
Razor-thin margins have delayed the race calls, but as noted above, Cindy Holscher likely will be our next governor. Chris Mann will be our next attorney general.
Add those 20 bonus Democrats in the House, and Kansas state government has jerked toward to the left. While outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly won two terms, she didn’t have the advantage of a 68-57 split in the House or a counterpart from her party in the attorney general’s office. Few followers of Kansas politics would have predicted such a result — certainly not me.
Forecasting what this means for the Kansas government is difficult because we haven’t been in this situation for decades. Kansas Republicans have come to view the Statehouse as their possession, rather than a gift loaned to them by voters a few years at a time.
Much will depend on how Republican senators react. They still hold a 31-9 supermajority in their chamber. Losing gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson could return as president and dedicate himself to thwarting Holscher’s ambitions. He may well be successful. On the other hand, without her cooperation and the assistance of House Democrats, Masterson can’t pass much on his own.
 
Patrick Lopez, a long-time Dodge City resident and educator, protests the presence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
West Kansas revenge
Early last month, I asked whether Trump might harbor a secret hatred for incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall. Trump’s administration had unleashed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to tear through western Kansas neighborhoods, spreading terror among residents.
Trump subsequently visited Kansas twice, supposedly showing support for the embattled senator. But you still have to wonder after looking at the enormous vote swings out in western Kansas, where Ford, Finney and Seward counties all voted for Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Preliminary vote totals over at Secretary of State Scott Schwab’s website show voters in those counties turned out in unexpected numbers for Holscher and Mann as well.
Perhaps Trump secretly disliked Masterson and Kobach too!
 
Rep. Adam Smith stands on the House floor on April 10, 2025. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Property tax proposal
State Rep. Adam Smith, a Weskan Republican, offered this intriguing suggestion via his Facebook page:


“As we celebrate the end of the political campaign ads, I’m thinking we should have a surcharge / tax on political advertising that goes into a fund that is then 100% directly sent back to each homeowner in the form of a property tax rebate.”


Smith said he only ran for reelection after Masterson blamed him for the demise of a property tax bill last session. So perhaps he has the bipartisan credibility needed to make this happen.
“I’ve been working on a bill!! For real!!” state Sen. Tim Shallenburger in an over-punctuated response.
As a former state treasurer, Shallenburger brings real policy chops to the discussion.
Lawmakers have other priorities, of course. But after the 2026 campaign season, who wouldn’t take a serious look?
 
Clay Wirestone appears as a guest on the Kansas Reflector podcast on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Optimistic note
I’ll admit that I’ve swung toward the cranky side since Tuesday night.
Those of us in the opinion trade must comprehend a historic event in real time, while keeping our wits about us. Partisan celebrations or acrimony can skew perspective. My beliefs persist, regardless of how any single election turns out.
Enough of my bellyaching. As I told the League of Women Voters of Johnson County on Saturday morning, the practical outcomes of this election are clear. Over the next two years, Kansas will pass an abortion ban. It will not pass a school voucher scheme that takes from the poor and gives to the rich. It will not cut school funding over ideological flapdoodle.
Such basic good government shouldn’t be partisan. Unfortunately for everyday Kansans, conservative Republican leaders have worked ruthlessly to gouge and stifle state services. We’ve lost precious time to arrant nonsense.
The threats have’t been vanquished. But thanks to the dedicated efforts of our states voters, they’ve been delayed a good while. That’s worth a nod of appreciation this Monday.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: School referendum passage declines amid public school advocates’ high hopes for new state government
description: Wisconsin voters approved about 55% of school referendum requests across the state — a majority passage rate that still marked a significant decline from previous years. Of 79 referendum questions on ballots last week, 44 referendum were approved and 35 failed. In April, 61% of referendum requests passed. According to the Wisconsin Policy Forum, in […]
text:
A hallway in La Follette High School in Madison. (Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Wisconsin voters approved about 55% of school referendum requests across the state — a majority passage rate that still marked a significant decline from previous years. Of 79 referendum questions on ballots last week, 44 referendum were approved and 35 failed.
In April, 61% of referendum requests passed. According to the Wisconsin Policy Forum, in 2024, there was a 70% approval rate; in 2022, there was an 80% approval rate; and in 2020, there was a 85% approval rate.
Schools have come to depend on ballot measures asking local property taxpayers to meet their costs including paying electric bills, building maintenance and program offerings as well as  providing pay and benefits to teachers and staff.
Wisconsin Public Education Network Executive Director Heather DuBois Bourenane called the results a “mixed bag.” 
“Green Bay desperately needed that referendum. Dodgeville, you know, had to go to referenda four times in order to pass one, and I mean the referendum they passed still leaves them in a pretty precarious fiscal situation, but at least they aren’t facing the same kind of cuts and shortfalls that they would have otherwise,” DuBois Bourenane said. “Most of them did pass, but the ones that didn’t are just gutting.” 
Schools in districts where  referendum requests failed she said, will be considering cuts to services and staff or consolidating schools or even dissolving their districts.
The latter option became a reality for one school district in Wisconsin right after the elections. 
The State Board approved a dissolution request for Hustisford School District in Dodge County. The tiny district had struggled financially in part due to a lack of state funding and repeated failed referendum requests. After the fifth failed referendum in April, it started the dissolution process.
State Superintendent Jill Underly said in a statement that dissolution “is a casualty of decades of an antiquated, broken school funding formula that has failed to keep pace with the costs of educating our children.” 
State support for public schools has declined dramatically over the last 15 years. Ahead of the election, 62% of Wisconsin public schools received notice from the state Department of Public Instruction that they would receive less aid for 2026-27 school year than in the prior year. The current state budget did not provide any increase in funding for 2026 or 2027.
Underly said in a statement that following Tuesday’s elections she is hopeful that the state is in a position to make “meaningful change” to the way Wisconsin funds its schools. 
“While I am optimistic about what the outcomes of yesterday’s election mean for the future of public education in Wisconsin, that optimism does not undermine the reality that too many communities are forced to make an unfair decision,” Underly said. “The school funding formula is broken, and it has failed our children, our schools, and entire communities for decades. Wisconsin’s public schools cannot continue to rely on referenda to provide the educational opportunities all students deserve.”
Underly said she looks forward to working with Wisconsin’s elected leaders as Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley and members of a Democratic-controlled state Assembly and Senate prepare to take office.
“There’s just like a lot of energy right now about the possibility of a more democratic co-governance that could be possible,” DuBois Bourenane said. The Democrats who will lead state government “seem truly committed to listening to people and to delivering a budget that reflects their needs,” she said. “That’s something we haven’t seen in this state in a really long time. We can fix school funding for real. We can actually get to the root of the problem and set this course straight and undo the damage that’s been done in previous administrations.” 
Among the actions DuBois Bourenane hopes to see from the new administration and Legislature are the repeal of Wisconsin’s union-busting law, Act 10, and making the cost of the state’s school voucher program public on property taxpayers’ bills. She said Crowley and lawmakers could also get to work on funding issues before the next state budget, suggesting  that a bill to provide 60% funding to special education could be among the first that Crowley signs. 
“The fact that about half of the referend this all didn’t pass means we’re going to see a ton of referenda in the spring again, and we shouldn’t have to wait for another budget to go into action to help the schools that are struggling now,” she said. 
It’s unclear how fast Democrats plan to move on education funding. 
Crowley campaigned on increasing funding to the state’s public schools, including moving the state toward reimbursing districts for 90% of the cost of special education, but he has said that he would want to bring together a blue ribbon commission to examine Wisconsin’s taxation system, including the role of property taxes in school funding. 
Crowley is not the only Democratic leader to suggest there could be additional study on changes to school funding. 
Senate Democratic Leader Dianne Hesselbein (D-Middleton), who will likely become the next Senate majority leader, said in late September that Democrats will increase school funding in the next state budget, but added that though she said changing the state’s school funding formula could be a “multi-year” process.
“We’re also looking at a long-term goal of seeing what other states are doing and how they are funding their public schools,” she said. “But that’s going to take probably a multi-year task to try to figure that all out and talking to our friends in Minnesota, Michigan, Illinois.”
Crowley also said he supports repealing Act 10, but he wants his administration to look at the impact on taxes.
“We’re going to couple all of this with a blue ribbon commission bringing Democrats, Republicans, tax experts, local units of government, business leaders, as well as labor unions to the table to focus on that long-term fix,”  Crowley recently told WISN-12. “We know that there are going to be a lot of people who continue to attack our workers across the state of Wisconsin, but our job is to make sure that this is a place they can see a future that they can afford.” 
DuBois Bourenane was not enthusiastic about the idea of another blue ribbon commission on school funding, saying it is the “last thing” Wisconsin needs. 
“We know exactly what the problem is. There is no mystery here. There is no need for additional research. There is no need to study this problem further, we have been studying and documenting what the problem is for decades,” DuBois Bourenane said, noting that Crowley was in the Legislature during the last blue ribbon commission. 
The last bipartisan blue ribbon commission on school funding was conducted nearly 10 years ago and took two years to complete its work. It provided a slate of recommendations to address the issues in the school funding system including indexing per pupil funding to inflation. Many of the recommendations went unaddressed by the Republican-led state Legislature. 
“Those recommendations sit unfulfilled on a dusty shelf, and he could just blow the dust off of that and put those into action if he wants. Those are still good recommendations,” DuBois Bourenane said. “We need to do a lot more than piecemeal solutions. We need to really overhaul the school finding formula, and we know how to do that.”

title: The 2nd District candidates agree LePage won. The ranked choice runoff still starts today.
description: The ranked choice runoff for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District starts today, even though the two candidates have agreed that former Gov. Paul LePage is Maine’s newest congressman.  The Maine Secretary of State’s Office announced Thursday that the election would head to ranked choice tabulation, after the Republican received 49.894% of votes. To avoid the ru[...]
text:
Sealed ballot boxes are wheeled in on the first day of the ranked-choice tabulation to determine the winners of three Maine primaries held on June 9, 2026. Officials in the Secretary of State’s office began conducting the count at the Maine Department of Public Safety in Augusta on June 12, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star)The ranked choice runoff for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District starts today, even though the two candidates have agreed that former Gov. Paul LePage is Maine’s newest congressman. 
The Maine Secretary of State’s Office announced Thursday that the election would head to ranked choice tabulation, after the Republican received 49.894% of votes. To avoid the runoff, he needed to get more than 50% of 2nd District votes. 
Despite Dunlap’s concession, 2nd District race still headed to ranked choice runoff

After the announcement, Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded the race, but the Secretary of State’s Office said state law still requires that they run the ranked choice tabulation.
The office said the ranked choice process would begin Monday at 10 a.m. in Augusta. 
The process is expected to take several days to complete, and the bulk of that time will be the secretary of state’s staff logging results from every ballot and checking multiple times to ensure the totals line up. Actually running the ranked choice tabulation formula produces results in a matter of minutes.
The tabulation process in Maine will be livestreamed on the Secretary of State’s YouTube page. The public is also invited to watch the process in-person.

title: Commentary: The election is over. The energy bills aren’t. Five priorities for Wisconsin’s new leadership.
description: Wisconsin voters have chosen a new governor and Democratic majorities in the Legislature. The campaigns have ended. The bills will not. Families and businesses still face rising utility costs. Communities are weighing enormous data center developments. Utilities are proposing billions in new power plants and transmission infrastructure. And too many Wisconsi[...]
text:
Wind turbines rise up above farmland near Middleton, Wisconsin. After last week's blue-wave election, the new governor and Legislature have a chance to transform the state's approach to energy.  (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)Wisconsin voters have chosen a new governor and Democratic majorities in the Legislature. The campaigns have ended. The bills will not.
Families and businesses still face rising utility costs. Communities are weighing enormous data center developments. Utilities are proposing billions in new power plants and transmission infrastructure. And too many Wisconsin families live in homes that are expensive to heat and cool.
Governor-elect David Crowley and the incoming Legislature have an opportunity to turn campaign promises into meaningful action. Energy affordability should be the North Star.
That means changing how Wisconsin plans its energy future, holds utilities accountable and invests in solutions that deliver lasting value.
Here are five priorities for the new administration and Legislature.
1. Require utilities to show their math before spending billions.
Wisconsin requires communities to plan for growth and infrastructure. Yet our statewide energy system lacks a comparable process for determining which investments are needed and provide the best value.
Instead, major power plants are largely evaluated one project at a time.
The Legislature should require integrated resource planning, bringing generation, transmission, battery storage, energy efficiency, distributed energy and demand flexibility into one transparent process.
Before approving multibillion-dollar investments, utilities should demonstrate how much electricity is needed, which alternatives were considered, how costs compare and who bears the risk if demand forecasts change.
The Public Service Commission should have the authority to demand these answers before committing customers to decades of costs.
Plan first. Spend second.
2. Make Big Tech pay its own way.
Data centers can bring investment, jobs and economic opportunity. Wisconsin should welcome development that delivers lasting benefits.
But growth should not come with a blank check.
A handful of large electricity users could drive billions in new generation, transmission and grid upgrades. Existing customers should not subsidize those investments or absorb the risks if projects are delayed, downsized or abandoned.
The Legislature should establish enforceable data center accountability standards requiring large users to pay the full infrastructure costs attributable to their operations, provide financial guarantees against stranded costs and bring additional clean energy onto the grid.
Data centers should disclose electricity and water requirements, demonstrate project viability and provide meaningful community participation and enforceable local benefits.
These protections must be established before infrastructure investments are approved.
The question is who pays, who benefits and who bears the risk.
3. Stop treating new methane gas plants as inevitable.
Wisconsin utilities are proposing billions in new methane gas infrastructure that could lock customers into decades of construction, financing and volatile fuel costs.
Growing electricity demand does not automatically justify new fossil fuel generation.
Before approving new gas plants, the PSC should require utilities to demonstrate that they have evaluated cost-effective alternatives, including renewables, battery storage, efficiency, demand response, virtual power plants and transmission improvements.
The new administration should strengthen oversight of utility demand forecasts, reliability claims and proposed investments.
Reliability is essential. But it requires comprehensive planning, not assumptions about which power plants must be built.
4. Put Wisconsin on a path to 100% clean electricity.
Illinois, Michigan and Minnesota have adopted clean electricity standards. Wisconsin should establish its own pathway by codifying a goal of 100% clean electricity by 2050.
The Legislature should pair that commitment with policies accelerating cost-effective renewable energy, storage, grid modernization and Wisconsin’s clean energy workforce and supply chains.
Wisconsin workers can build these projects. Manufacturers can supply the equipment. Communities can benefit from investment and jobs. And energy resources without ongoing fuel costs can reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices.
Clean energy is not simply an environmental priority. It is an affordability and economic development strategy. 
5. Lower bills through healthier, more efficient homes.
An affordable energy future begins at home.
More than half of Wisconsin homes were built before 1980. Many families face high utility bills because of inadequate insulation, outdated equipment or repairs that prevent energy improvements.
Wisconsin already has a proven solution in Focus on Energy. Program estimates show approximately $3.57 to $4.17 in benefits for every dollar invested, yet its funding rate has remained unchanged for 27 years.
The Legislature should double Focus on Energy funding and expand weatherization and efficiency assistance, particularly for low- and moderate-income households.
Wisconsin should also establish a dedicated Healthy Homes initiative, combining energy improvements with essential health and safety repairs, including moisture, ventilation and electrical problems.
The Clean Economy Coalition of Wisconsin’s Healthy Homes Campaign is helping connect families and small businesses with existing programs while building support for expanded investment.
At Wisconsin Environmental Initiative, our Green Built Home program has demonstrated that better buildings mean healthier families, stronger communities and lasting affordability.
Efficiency should be treated as infrastructure. The cheapest energy is often what we never need to generate.
Turn promises into measurable results.
These priorities are connected. Data centers influence electricity demand. Demand forecasts drive infrastructure investments. Those investments affect utility bills. Clean energy and efficiency can reduce costs and risks.
The new administration and Legislature should bring these issues together through a comprehensive energy affordability agenda, with clear legislative priorities, stronger PSC oversight and measurable progress on customer costs.
Wisconsin families deserve lower bills. Businesses need greater certainty. Communities deserve a voice. And economic development should strengthen our state without transferring unnecessary financial risks to existing customers.
Affordable, reliable electricity is fundamental to Wisconsin’s competitiveness and quality of life.
The campaigns have ended. Now comes the work of governing.
Plan first. Make Big Tech pay its own way. Invest in clean energy and healthier homes. Hold utilities accountable.
And make affordability the measure of success.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Data centers go 0-for-21 in ballot initiatives around Ohio
description: Ohio voters sharply rejected data centers in this year’s election. Around Ohio, 18 communities voted on whether to curb or ban data center developments. In all 18 communities, voters decided that, yes, that would be a good idea. In most, the results were resounding — like Harlem Globetrotters v. Washington Generals resounding. City leaders in […]
text:
An anti-data center sign.(Photo by Peter Hall/States Newsroom)Ohio voters sharply rejected data centers in this year’s election. Around Ohio, 18 communities voted on whether to curb or ban data center developments. In all 18 communities, voters decided that, yes, that would be a good idea.
In most, the results were resounding — like Harlem Globetrotters v. Washington Generals resounding. City leaders in Wilmington, the county seat of Clinton County, asked voters to rezone four parcels to allow data center development. Roughly 80% of voters rejected all four.
In the Lake County Village of Perry, more than 87% of voters backed an initiative requiring data centers that accept tax incentives to take out a bond, operating kind of like an insurance policy, to back up their promises of local tax revenue.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Voters in Piqua prohibited data centers within city limits by a 2-to-1 margin and didn’t stop there. They also recalled three city commissioners — including the mayor and vice-mayor — for approving a Meta data center in November last year.
From Conneaut in far Northeastern Ashtabula County to Trenton in Southwestern Butler County, nine communities passed initiatives modeled on the statewide data center moratorium Conserve Ohio organizers are trying to put on the ballot in 2027. That initiative would amend the state constitution to prohibit any data center drawing more than 25 megawatts a month.
In a press release, Conserve Ohio congratulated communities who voted against data center development, and warned elected officials that “You cannot look away now.”
“The above election results demonstrate that when communities have a say regarding the construction of a hyperscale data center in their local area, they overwhelmingly say no,” the group wrote. “Your oath is invoked. Stop the self-dealing, corporate fealty, and greed. Represent and serve the people who elected you.”
Conserve Ohio urged Ohio citizens to push state lawmakers to pass a 12-month moratorium on any data center development in Ohio during the lame duck session between now and the end of the year.
Upper Sandusky
Angela Huffman is a sixth-generation farmer in Northwest Ohio, and she heads up the national watchdog group Farm Action, which focuses on corporate consolidation in the food and agriculture sector. She explained data centers came onto their radar about a year ago, because of concerns about their impact on farmland.
“And then lo and behold,” Huffman said, “I read in the newspaper back in June of this year that a data center, a nearly $1 billion data center, was proposed here right outside Upper Sandusky, which is about 10 miles from my farm.”
Upper Sandusky is the county seat of Wyandot County, but it’s a small city with a population of less than 7,000 residents. In June, the company Smartland Energy proposed building a 150-megawatt natural gas plant on a 46-acre parcel. The idea was to build the powerplant first and then sell the power directly to a data center client on an adjacent 100-acre parcel.
Smartland emphasized it “would not build, own or run” the data center, and that the eventual end-user would still need city approval and hadn’t been pre-selected.
Huffman and other organizers began collecting signatures to oppose the project, and unlike many petition drives, she said their job was relatively easy.
“Really our challenge was just finding ways to get in front of people,” she said. “They already knew about the issue. They were already concerned about data centers. So fortunately, we didn’t have to first educate or raise awareness and educate about what the problem was. They already knew. We just had to get their names on these petitions in time.”
Huffman noted construction of a Louis Dreyfus Company soybean processing plant was already stretching local infrastructure, and a data center adding to the strain was a daunting prospect.
When Upper Sandusky voters went into the booth last Tuesday, nearly 77% of them approved a city charter amendment banning data centers within city limits.
Looking forward
In a Facebook post last Thursday, Smartland Energy seemingly acknowledged its project doesn’t have a future in Upper Sandusky. The company thanked the community and reiterated its belief in their proposal.
“At the same time,” it stated, “we value and respect the democratic process and the outcome of the charter amendment vote.”
“Our team will take some time to come together, reflect on this process, and discuss the outcome,” Smartland added. “If there is ever anything further to share, this will be the first place we communicate it.”
The drubbing data centers took in Ohio last Tuesday didn’t stop at the state line. Around the country, 47 initiatives were on the ballot to restrict data centers. Election officials are still counting votes for two of those contests, but according to the website Data Centers on the Ballot, 44 jurisdictions rejected data centers and just one welcomed them.
The day after the election, data center industry group Infrastructure for America released what it called a “good actor pledge”. It’s members, including Compass, Digital Realty, QTS and Vantage, committed to operate transparently, invest in their communities, and not be a drain on local power and water infrastructure.
Ohio Capital Journal sent an email to the Data Center Coalition seeking comment about Ohio’s results, but got no response.
To Huffman, the election results underscore the importance of communities having a voice in major developments like data centers. She stressed that she doesn’t oppose AI or development generally, but the way the industry has been operating feels “predatory.”
Between tax abatements for developers, and the lack of local protections or input, “it’s really been tilted in favor of big tech,” she said, “at the expense of Ohio.”
“I think that’s where a lot of the pushback started,” Huffman added. “If this had been more of a level playing field from the start, I don’t think there would have been as much opposition.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Democrats take control of Georgia’s powerful utility regulator
description: This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Beginning in January, three of the five officials on the Georgia Public Service Commission will be Democrats. It will be the first time the party has controlled the powerful energy regulation board in 30 years.  The commission, which […]
text:
Peter Hubbard, Democratic member of the Public Service Commission, joined Atlanta's former mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic candidate for Governor, at a press conference in downtown Marietta on Sept. 14, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderThis coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Beginning in January, three of the five officials on the Georgia Public Service Commission will be Democrats. It will be the first time the party has controlled the powerful energy regulation board in 30 years. 
The commission, which regulates utilities including the state’s largest electric provider, Georgia Power, has come under more scrutiny in recent years due to rising power bills and the high energy demands of data centers. 
On Tuesday, Peter Hubbard was re-elected to his seat and Shelia Edwards won her race for an open seat. The third Democrat, Alicia Johnson, was not up for election this year. Georgia PSC commissioners serve six-year terms.  
Now, Democrats say they plan to focus on affordability, clean energy and closer scrutiny of Georgia Power. 
“There’s a long laundry list of things that need to be looked into,” Hubbard said. “We’ll have to triage, in fact, and decide how best to move forward.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
One of his first priorities will be launching an affordability docket, he said — a series of hearings that would delve into the reasons for high power bills and ways to save customers money. Hubbard said he and his fellow Democrats also plan to bring close scrutiny to upcoming Georgia Power requests around making more energy and adjusting customer rates. 
But any changes, especially to power bills, will likely take time. 
“We may not be able to expect immediate effects on our wallets,” said Emory University associate professor Kristin Phillips, who studies energy burden and the PSC. “But I think we can expect immediate change in the types of decisions that are made.”
Affordability and high energy bills were driving issues in the campaigns both this year and last year, the two elections that together resulted in the new Democratic majority on the commission.
“We knew that we had to connect the dots between energy and affordability,” Brionté McCorkle of Georgia Conservation Voters said during a media briefing after the election. Her group campaigned for the Democratic candidates and worked to draw attention to the PSC elections. “It’s not just this obscure regulatory body like it used to be treated. Its decisions directly affect household budgets, communities, health and our energy future.”
Chris Womack, the CEO of Southern Company, Georgia Power’s parent company, also acknowledged the central importance of affordability during the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Thursday. But Womack said he’s confident the utility can address those concerns with the new commissioners.
“If you look at what we have been doing with rate freezes, with benefits, with how we are providing benefits from growth to customers — existing customers — as well as to the communities, we think that’s a strong platform to stand on,” he said.
Data centers, power bills and transparency
Since the data center boom in Georgia began, Georgia Power has maintained that the increased revenue from the energy-hungry facilities would more than pay for the new infrastructure needed to serve them. The utility argues that should keep rates lower for residential and small business customers. The utility calls this “downward pressure.” It doesn’t mean, though, that rates will go down for everyone else, but rather that any increases would be offset by the influx of revenue from data centers. 
The utility recently doubled down on that promise as part of its deal to serve a massive new OpenAI data center planned near Savannah. The deal, Georgia Power said, would bring $15 not of savings but of downward pressure per month for what Georgia Power calls the “typical” residential customer. 
Georgia Power also credited the increased revenue from data centers for the temporary rate freeze approved last year. But the rate freeze received criticism from some consumer and environmental groups because when it was announced, the deal essentially preempted previously planned PSC hearings that would have given advocates a chance to verify the utility’s financial claims. Advocates felt the process left them unable to confirm whether the company was delivering on its promises and fully shielding ordinary customers from data center costs. 
It’s part of a broader criticism often leveled at the PSC and Georgia Power: lack of transparency. 
The OpenAI contract was entirely redacted; a summary was provided to the public after the deal was approved. Specific details on other issues – from service contracts, to deals to buy energy, to construction costs – are often redacted from the utility’s public filings under the auspices of trade secrecy. Critics argue that while much of the information is indeed trade-secret, the redactions may go too far, and that PSC proceedings and Georgia Power operations in general should be clearer and more open to the public. Commission chair Jason Shaw acknowledged in an interview with WABE earlier this year that the commission needs to “do a better job of forcing” Georgia Power to make more details of its contracts public.
“I absolutely think transparency is potentially one of the biggest impacts here,” said Phillips of the election results. “It has been often on advocates to push on the way that the PSC communicates about the decisions that it’s making, and I’m hoping that there will be more clarity and transparency.”
The Democrats on the commission have promised to bring increased scrutiny to the next rate-setting process, scheduled for 2028, along with Georgia Power’s long-term plans to make and deliver energy, its forecasts about rising demand and other issues. Hubbard has also proposed conducting a rate case for the state’s natural gas utilities, which he said hasn’t been done in over a decade. And he said they’ll push for other changes going forward.
“We’ll continue with an agenda next year and the year after that to take advantage of this four-year period when we have the majority and can push for long-lasting reforms and shifting the direction of the state in terms of energy,” Hubbard said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan voters support more education funding, but how to pay for it is complicated
description: Jen Stroven, an organizer for Kalamazoo’s Yes For Families campaign, knew what she was up against: ‘Affordability, affordability, affordability.’  Asking voters to raise their own taxes to lower child care costs, expand access, and raise teacher wages may have seemed like a tall order at a time when the increased cost of living is a […]
text:
Getty ImagesJen Stroven, an organizer for Kalamazoo’s Yes For Families campaign, knew what she was up against: ‘Affordability, affordability, affordability.’ 
Asking voters to raise their own taxes to lower child care costs, expand access, and raise teacher wages may have seemed like a tall order at a time when the increased cost of living is a top issue on voters’ minds. But Stroven was confident the 0.5-mill property tax proposal would pass and she was right. In August, 63% of voters in Kalamazoo County approved the eight-year initiative that will add an average of $50 a month to their property tax bills. 

Stroven said that even for those voters who didn’t have young kids, they were able to see the economic benefit for communities and businesses that are losing workers because of lack of affordable childcare. She said they also understood how far-reaching the impact could be from the benefits to families to childcare workers, to the kids themselves. 
“It seemed for most folks to be a worthwhile investment,” Stroven said. 
The success of the Kalamazoo millage may come at a particularly cash-strapped time for voters but its passage is part of a larger trend both statewide and nationally of a shift in thinking from childcare and early childhood education as a personal responsibility to a public good. Kent County approved an early childhood millage in 2018; Leelanau County followed in 2019.
If voters can coalesce around early childhood education as a social good, whether or not funding for K-12 education can receive similar support is a little more complicated. 
Jen Stroven from the Kalamazoo Yes for Families Campaign. (Photo provided)
The legacy of Proposal A
For better or worse, K-12 educational funding in Michigan changed dramatically in 1994. Before, each school district relied heavily on local property taxes for funding. Unsurprisingly this led to massive inequities: Cities with a lot of property wealth could easily fund high teacher salaries, extensive programming and small class sizes with even smaller tax rates, while districts with low property values and rural communities were underfunded. 
In late 1993, the state Legislature removed the local property tax system, followed several months later by the voter-approved Proposal A constitutional amendment restructuring how Michigan funds K-12 public school operations. 
Since then, the Legislature distributes the exact same amount for each student in all schools through the School Aid Fund. Revenue for the fund comes mostly from sales taxes with small portions of revenue from income and property taxes.

Inequities still exist: Districts can pass voter-approved millages for capital expenses, such as school bonds and sinking funds to build new buildings or improve old ones. This means that some districts have state-of-the-art school buildings while students in other districts are stuck in crumbling schools.
David Arsen | Michigan State University
But all Michigan districts are legally restricted from asking voters to fund operational expenses like hiring more teachers, increasing salaries or even basics like paying a building’s utility bills. This funding paradox can create an incongruent situation like what’s currently playing out in Ann Arbor: a budget crisis with teacher layoffs while new school buildings are erected from a 2018 millage. 
On one hand, the Proposal A funding model has created more solidarity among districts, said David Arsen, a Michigan State University professor who specializes in education policy and school finance. But the downside, he says, is that communities lose the ability to respond locally to their own needs even if voters would be willing to tax themselves as they were in Kalamazoo. 
Why are schools still underfunded? 
In July, Michigan lawmakers celebrated a per-pupil funding increase from $10,050 to $10,300, along with other notable educational investments from the School Aid Fund, including an expansion of the Great Start Readiness Program to fund PreK for All and free school meals. Still, school funding hasn’t kept up with inflation and the changing economy. 
A recent poll commissioned by the K-12 Alliance of Michigan found that half of surveyed voters said that their local school districts have funding shortages for the resources they need.
Not keeping up with inflation
While $10,300 per student may sound like a lot, that number hasn’t kept pace with inflation according to research from the Education Policy Innovation Collaborative at MSU.  When adjusted for inflation, Michigan now spends less on school operations than it did decades ago. In 2002, the School Aid Fund provided an inflation-adjusted average of $13,858 per student.

 Decreased enrollment 
As a result of declining birth rates, population loss and other factors, public school enrollment in Michigan has declined by nearly 20%, or more than 335,000 students, since 2002. 
Tying funding to the number of students means that when enrollment drops, money disappears, even if costs increase. Schools have many fixed costs that can’t fluctuate with enrollment. A loss of even 20 students across all grade levels means a district loses hundreds of thousands of dollars while its operational costs, such as heating and cooling, running bus routes and paying school nurses, remain fixed or even increase with inflation. 
Compounding enrollment losses over several years force districts to cut essential staff and increase class sizes just to keep their budget balanced, even as per-pupil funding numbers are increased. 

 The problem with sales tax
Arsen explains that because the state sales tax is the primary source of revenue for the School Aid Fund, the education system loses out when there is a shift in consumer behavior and the tax code doesn’t keep up.
“The sales tax, which is the main source of revenue to the school aid fund, is based on the goods economy. There are a whole host of things in services that are not taxed. And so as the economy itself shifts from goods-producing to more services, that source of income doesn’t keep pace,” Arsen said. 
 Where is the money going to come from?

The good news for schools is that voters generally agree that funding education should be a priority, and as supporters of  the Kalamazoo millage demonstrated — a case can be made that well-educated kids are essential for the future of the state. However, figuring out where the money will come from remains a challenge. 
“We can get consensus in Michigan on equitable and adequate funding. What we have not been able to do yet is get agreement on where the revenues will come in order to fund that,”  Arsen said.
Molly Sweeney, organizing director of 482Forward, a member of the Invest in MI Kids ballot proposal coalition tells reporters the group plans to begin circulating petitions. July 31, 2025 | Photo By Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance


The 2025 Invest in MI Kids campaign was an attempt at a solution. The campaign aimed to get a constitutional amendment on the 2026 ballot to place a 5% surcharge on single filers earning more than $500,000 and joint filers earning over $1 million. 
The initiative would have raised between $1.5 and $2 billion annually to lower student-to-teacher ratios, expand technical education and improve teacher retention. 

The campaign faced several obstacles, including pushback and procedural delays along with a high signature threshold. Though the campaign collected more than 250,000 signatures, it fell short of the goal and suspended operations in March, saying it would look toward the 2028 election cycle instead. 
Despite not making this year’s ballot, campaign manager Jessica Newman, co-director of the Michigan Education Justice Coalition, still thinks there’s a path to future success.
Jess Newman with Invest in MI Kids (Photo provided)
“This is a state that is ready to tax the rich, it’s ready to fund our public goods and services, and I wouldn’t take our failure to get on the ballot as evidence of that at all,” she said.  
Newman is not alone in that belief. Stroven and Arsen agreed that education funding is increasingly a bipartisan issue in Michigan. 
As Invest in MI Kids looks to the 2028 ballot, the campaign is now considering several other funding options beyond an increased income tax on high earners. Funding options that the campaign proposed in a survey to past canvassers include repealing data center property and sales tax exemptions, raising the corporate income tax rate, introducing a wealth proceeds tax, introducing a digital advertising tax and extending the sales tax to include services. 
Disclosure: The author was a volunteer signature collector for the campaign in 2025.
Voters in Kalamazoo and other counties approved taxes to pay for childcare. If Invest in MI Kids manages to get a proposal on the ballot next year, will Michiganders vote to fund education statewide? Public opinion seems to indicate they might. 
According to the EPIC survey, 65% of voters support an increase in education spending and put it on the top of their list of priorities, above even healthcare and fixing the roads.  
Newman remains hopeful. “I don’t have kids, but I understand that public schools are a public good that help every single person in the community.”
Support for this reporting came from The Better Life Lab at New America.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Incoming Dem Ohio Secretary of State will do what she can to roll back GOP voting restrictions
description: As Democrats swept to historic victories Tuesday, a win in the Ohio Secretary of State race might start the process of rolling back years of Republican restrictions on voting that were predicated on voter fraud that didn’t exist. Allison Russo, a member of the state House of Representatives, defeated Republican Robert Sprague by 3.5 percentage […]
text:
Ohio Secretary of State-elect Allison Russo. (Photo by Nick Evans/ Ohio Capital Journal)As Democrats swept to historic victories Tuesday, a win in the Ohio Secretary of State race might start the process of rolling back years of Republican restrictions on voting that were predicated on voter fraud that didn’t exist.
Allison Russo, a member of the state House of Representatives, defeated Republican Robert Sprague by 3.5 percentage points to become secretary of state, the office that oversees Ohio’s elections and business registration.
Now she has a chance to continue a fight she began while she was in the legislature — to protect voting access for Ohioans.
“The thing that motivated me (to run) was understanding how important this office is for voting rights and for access to our elections,” Russo said in a phone interview. “I’ve known for a long time that this is an office I wanted to run for, and that we needed someone there to be an advocate for voters and voting.”
She was elected as part of a rout that broke total Republican control statewide offices in Ohio and left the GOP with only one statewide, non-judicial office — that of state auditor. 
As the GOP gained power in Ohio over the past 20 years, its leaders have entrenched that power through measures that critics said were antidemocratic. 
They severely gerrymandered the state legislature and Ohio’s congressional districts and then ignored seven orders of the Ohio Supreme Court saying that the gerrymanders were unconstitutional. 
And outgoing Secretary Frank LaRose repeatedly ratcheted down voting access on claims that the goal was to fight voter fraud. Yet his office’s own numbers demonstrated that it only might have happened 0.0005% of the time in the 2020 election. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And more recent reporting for the Capital Journal shows there have been just nine convictions for illegal voting out of 35 million votes. That’s 0.0000003 convictions per vote cast.
Nevertheless, LaRose implemented rules and Republicans passed laws that shortened the early voting calendar, shortened deadlines around absentee voting and restricted the number of drop boxes and early-voting sites to one per county — regardless of whether the county is home to millions who tend to vote for Democrats or just 13,000 who tend to vote for Republicans.
Ohio Republicans also enacted one of the strictest voter ID laws in the United States.
All of those things culminated in the last night of early voting in Columbus, where voters had to stand in line for at least an hour after the polls had officially closed.
Russo said such waits are unacceptable, but as secretary of state, she has to deal with the law as it is.
“We have to work with existing state law whether I like that existing state law or not,” she said. “That said, we have a secretary of state (LaRose) who we’ve seen go beyond the plain language of the law and sometimes make existing, unfavorable law even worse. 
“So we are going to be looking very closely at the directives that have been previously issued. We’re going to work with our local elections officials to understand which ones are problematic to implement because they’re unclear, the legality may be problematic, or there are resource issues. That will be one of the first orders of business.”
As for drop boxes and early voting sites and hours, Russo said she’ll do what she can.
“There is some discretion for the secretary of state over the hours and how you use those days and the hours that are available to voters,” she said. “We’re going to be looking at what we can do there, because I share the concern that many Ohioans had when they saw those long lines. We do not want voters to be discouraged if they show up. And they should not have to wait that long.”
The secretary of state also has considerable power over the mechanics of citizen-initiated laws and constitutional amendments. She ensures they follow the single-subject rule and otherwise pass legal muster — including by verifying petition signatures.
And crucially, she proposes the language that will appear on the ballot to the Ohio Ballot Board.
In 2024, a group led by former Ohio Supreme Court Justice Maureen O’Connor, a Republican, proposed a constitutional amendment that sought to end gerrymandering by creating an independent, bipartisan panel to draw legislative and congressional districts. 
LaRose proposed three pages of ballot language with a title claiming that under the amendment, the panel was “required to gerrymander” the districts. Republicans on the ballot board adopted the language and the amendment failed in the same election that gained Donald Trump a second term as president.
There has been talk of trying to get a similar amendment on the ballot ahead of the 2030 census. Russo said it could be one of several in the next two years.
“I suspect there will be a number of ballot issues that will come forward over the next couple of years to address many of these concerns that voters have in this space,” she said. “Whether it be redistricting (or gerrymandering) reform, or voting rights — or it could be education funding — I suspect it will be a number of issues. As secretary of state, my involvement will be when those issues come forward.”
Would she commit to proposing straightforward, unbiased ballot language regardless of the content of the statute or amendment?
“Absolutely,” Russo said. “I talked a lot about that on the campaign trail — the need to have a more transparent process with ballot language. There has to be ample public notice about the ballot language to keep it simple and clear and easily understood. 
“Because listen, when you complicate ballot language, not only does it confuse voters, it also contributes to these long lines when voters have to stand there and read a lot of language and try to comprehend what it means.”

title: Report shows Ohio has permanent housing beds for less than 10% of people experiencing homelessness
description: Ohio only has enough permanent housing beds for 8% of all Ohioans experiencing homelessness, according to a new report.  In total, Ohio has 935 available permanent housing beds, according to a new report from the National Alliance to End Homelessness. “(Homeless service providers are) providing critical life-saving services to people in need of housing on a [...]
text:
File photo from Derek Miles for Colorado Newsline, States Newsroom.Ohio only has enough permanent housing beds for 8% of all Ohioans experiencing homelessness, according to a new report. 
In total, Ohio has 935 available permanent housing beds, according to a new report from the National Alliance to End Homelessness.
“(Homeless service providers are) providing critical life-saving services to people in need of housing on a day-to-day basis, and that work is made much more difficult by the fact that they don’t actually have the resources to do that work effectively,” said Daniel Soucy, research analyst at National Alliance to End Homelessness. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ohio has less than one bed per every ten people experiencing homelessness, according to the report. 
“We would never ask an emergency room doctor to do surgery without a hospital room to do that surgery in, but we consistently ask homeless service providers to try and end homelessness without enough housing and enough shelter to do that,” Soucy said. 
Marcus Roth, spokesperson for the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio, said the report is concerning. 
“Funding and resources for Ohio’s homelessness system is being dwarfed by increasing need,” he said. 
“The real problem is the lack of resources for the system, combined with economic factors such as rising rents that are making options for people to avoid homelessness scarcer and scarcer.” 
In 2024, 32,000 Ohioans entered the homeless system, but less than half of them were able to get into permanent housing, Roth said. 
“Ohio’s homeless system is effective at getting people out of homelessness with very few resources, but it can’t keep up with the flow of people into homelessness,” he said. 
There were 12,196 people experiencing homelessness in Ohio in 2025 — a 3% increase from 2024, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development annual Homelessness Assessment Report. 
HUD’s Point-in-Time count are one-night estimates of sheltered and unsheltered people experiencing homelessness that took place in January 2025. 
About 20% of those experiencing homelessness in Ohio were unsheltered, according to HUD’s report. 
“It’s unsafe,” Soucy said. “It has impacts on people’s long-term health, and it’s an issue that we need to address urgently.” 
There has been a persistent shortage of shelter beds for more than a decade, Soucy said. 
“Asking service providers to end unsheltered homelessness, to find everybody a place to live when those resources just don’t exist, is not possible,” he said.
Ohio has about 63 shelter beds available per 100 people experiencing unsheltered homelessness, Soucy said. 
No state had homeless response systems with enough permanent housing for everyone experiencing homelessness at the time of HUD’s Point-in-Time count.
“We’re asking service providers to end homelessness with not even nearly enough resources,” Soucy said. 
Permanent housing ends homelessness, the housing advocates said.  
“What that usually looks like is private apartments that are owned by private landlords collaborating with homeless services agencies, so that they will help accept clients, people that are coming out of shelter,” Roth said. 
“What’s happened, though, with the increase in rent prices we’ve seen the last several years is that fewer and fewer landlords are willing to do that because they can make so much more money by just going to the private market, raising rents, and it’s leaving a real dearth of options for getting people out of homelessness.”
Ohio has a shortage of 266,000 affordable and available rental units, according to the 2026 Gap Report by the National Low Income Housing Coalition and COHHIO. 
A full-time Ohio worker needs to be making at least $23.82 an hour to be able to afford a “modest” two-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition and COHHIO’s annual Out of Reach report.
Local, state, and federal lawmakers need to invest more in homeless response systems and permanent housing, Soucy said. 
“We need to ensure that there is enough permanent housing for everybody who is experiencing homelessness,” he said. “That means investments and resources and funding for these systems.”
