name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Auditor raises eyebrows after signing tax deeds for a friend
description: Two state lawmakers are raising questions after the state auditor appears to have stepped to fix a deed issue for a friend.
text:
A West Virginia Watch investigation found West Virginia Auditor Mark Hunt’s signature on tax deeds, a move outside of state law governing the sale of delinquent tax properties. (Photo illustration by Amelia Ferrell Knisely)Two state lawmakers are raising questions after the state auditor appears to have stepped to fix a deed issue for a friend.  
The West Virginia state auditor is the state’s bookkeeper and responsible for rooting out fraud, waste and graft within both state and local governments. And in recent years, the auditor has been placed in charge of handling the sale of properties with delinquent taxes. 
But several property transactions in Kanawha and Boone counties show Auditor Mark Hunt may have stepped outside the bounds of the law to sell properties to a Charleston-based attorney who has amassed a land empire throughout the state. 
And records show that same attorney also worked for the Auditor’s Office.
West Virginia Watch, responding to news tips, searched land databases and visited a county clerk’s office to look for deeds with Hunt’s signature. It found that Hunt, a former state senator elected to the office in 2024, personally signed nine tax deeds between March and June 2025.  
State law governing the sale of delinquent tax properties, meaning properties lost because the owner didn’t pay their taxes, states that the deputy land commissioner – not the auditor – is supposed to sign those deeds. 
Hunt said when he came into the office in 2025, the land division that handles the deeds was in disarray, with files upon files of deeds in boxes. When Hunt’s office received a phone call from Robert L. Johns, a bankruptcy attorney, asking about deeds that had not yet been signed, the auditor said he became concerned that the office would be sued if the problem wasn’t fixed. 
A spokesperson for the prior Auditor, now Attorney General JB McCuskey, declined to comment about the state of the office. 
“This is our fault,” Hunt said. “So seeing inequity, I made a decision that I believe the 500,000 people who voted for me gave me that to make a judgment call. I made a judgment call to issue the deeds. 
“There’s no nefarious things here,” Hunt added “Frankly, it’s something I forgot even happened until this tempest in a teapot has come up in the last couple weeks.” 
But state code already addresses what should happen when the Auditor’s Office fails to provide the deed in a timely fashion. The person who bought it must take the deputy land commissioner to court. 
Records show two of the nine deeds were signed beyond a deadline mandated by state law, which Hunt said was due to the disorganized state of the office. 
Sen. Ryan Weld, R-Brooke, speaks on the Senate floor on Feb. 27, 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Sen. Ryan Weld, R-Brooke, is an attorney who deals with property rights and has lent a hand in rewriting how the state responds to owners who don’t pay their taxes. 
“It clearly states that deeds for people who purchase properties at these tax sales are issued and signed by the deputy commissioner,” Weld said. 
When a West Virginia landowner fails to pay property taxes, the county can seize the property for back taxes. Prior to changes in 2022, this was handled by the local sheriff. Now, the state auditor’s office handles the sale. An outside party can bid to buy the deed, at which point they have to notify the current owner. If the current owner doesn’t pay up on their taxes or respond, the outside party can then buy the deed to the property outright. 
Hunt’s cursive signature on the documents and the issuance of deeds to someone employed in the auditor’s office is extremely troubling to Weld. 
“On its face, it looks as if it’s intentional. And so you have to ask the question: Why?” Weld said.
Hunt defended his signature on the deeds. 
“The deputy commissioner works under and through me and through my authority,” Hunt said. “It would be foolish to think that the commissioner’s boss couldn’t sign the same deed, or any other matter in the office … I can sign whatever I need to sign to make the office work.” 
Hunt also pointed to a different piece of state code to support the practice he said he only did for Johns.  
Seventeen thousand deeds come through the auditor’s office a year, he said. 
Hunt, a lawyer by trade, added that “common law” protects his right to sign the deeds regardless of what the state code says. None of the allegations are criminal, he said.
“If someone would have a problem with me signing that deed instead of the deputy commissioner, someone has the right to go to circuit court and have it set aside,” Hunt said. 
Weld said this isn’t a paperwork issue – peoples’ homes are at stake. 
“You always have to be extremely cautious when you’re crafting legislation or statutes that affect people’s property rights and their ownership in it, and so that’s why we (lawmakers) went the painstaking lengths when we revised all of this several years ago to ensure that we were taking into account those rights,” Weld said. “You don’t want to see someone lose their property or lose their house simply because they didn’t pay their taxes.”
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha (Photo by Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, is the president of Empower Oversight, a nonprofit law firm that specializes in whistleblower cases and investigating government corruption. He said the deeds and Hunt’s explanation are concerning. 
“The law isn’t a buffet a public official can pick and choose from at will. The code here explicitly limits when the Auditor’s office can issue a deed,” he said. “If they make a mistake and should have issued a deed earlier, the remedy for that is to apply to a judge for execution of the deed, as state code requires.” 
Mark Hunt has served as West Virginia State Auditor since January 2025. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely for West Virginia Watch)
Hunt signed deeds for employee in auditor’s office
The nine deeds signed by Hunt went to MAPA LLC, a landholding company incorporated under Patricia Johns, the wife of Robert Johns. 
Both Johnses are listed as incorporators of a number of limited liability companies that hold hundreds of parcels of land throughout the state, with a total appraised value of $38 million. 
“I’ve known Bob for many years. He’s been a friend for years,” Hunt said, calling him an expert in the land process. Johns typically buys “scrub land,” like hillsides or creek beds that residents lost due to back taxes, Hunt explained.
“Over the years, he has bought a lot of land, and he pays a lot of taxes to the state of West Virginia because this is what the selling of this delinquent land’s about,” he said. 
Johns did not respond to multiple email interview requests for this story.
During the 2024 election, Patricia Johns donated $1,000 to Hunt’s campaign, as she did in his 2022 run for state Senate. 
The West Virginia State Checkbook, an online repository of how state finances are spent, shows Robert Johns worked at the auditor’s office in 2025, the latest calendar year available, and was paid a little more than $14,000. 
Hunt said he brought Johns into the auditor’s office to deal with McDowell County’s potential insolvency in 2024. Johns, a U.S. bankruptcy trustee, worked as the receiver for McDowell County to sort through the impoverished county’s financial issues. 
“We kept him on the payroll because there’s other towns that have become insolvent and have lost their charters, and that’s just a function that we provide,” Hunt said. “We got Bob as kind of a deal.”
Johns also works for the auditor’s office as a consultant on land issues, Hunt said.
Records show MAPA was buying delinquent property through July 2026.
Leavitt called the transfers, and the relationship between Johns and Hunt “cronyism.” 
“Mark Hunt’s claims that he had to correct a mistake made before he arrived don’t match up with evidence that he continued illegally approving deeds months into his tenure,” Leavitt said. 
Hunt said he wasn’t cutting a friend a break. He said there are six people, including Johns, buying 90% of the delinquent land throughout the state. The fact that he intervened to correct issues with Johns’ property isn’t unusual. 
“I don’t care if it’s Bob Johns, Bob Smith, Tom Johns, Tom Smith,” Hunt said. “If they had the same issue, I would have done the same thing.”
This isn’t the first time Hunt’s office has come under scrutiny. 
Earlier this year, journalist Kyle Vass reported Hunt hired state Sen. Jay Taylor, R-Taylor, on a contract basis to work at the Auditor’s Office, after being told by  Attorney General JB McCuskey that full time state government work by a sitting lawmaker was barred by the state constitution. 
Taylor said he was unaware there was an issue and was told by Hunt that everything was fine. 
In late October, Brad McElhinny of Metro News reported that the Auditor’s Office was served a federal grand jury subpoena. 
“Those federal subpoenas contained a clause that we’re not supposed to talk about the contents of,” Hunt said. “I don’t know what they’re doing, but I will tell you that no one’s even talked to me.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: DeSoto County, a Republican stronghold, key to Scott Colom’s midterm election performance
description: President Donald Trump embraces Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith during his rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
If Democrat Scott Colom ultimately wins Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race, upsetting Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, he needs to send a special thank you to the Memphis suburb of DeSoto County.
Surprisingly, it appears Colom will win DeSoto County, long viewed as one of the state’s Republican strongholds. But more important than the DeSoto victory for Colom is the vote totals in the county.
In the 2024 presidential election, Republican Donald Trump garnered 48,064 votes in DeSoto County to 29,023 for Democrat Kamala Harris.
When all the votes from Tuesday’s election are finally counted in the coming days, Colom will ultimately match Harris’ vote total in DeSoto County or fall just short of it. By the same token, Hyde-Smith garnered fewer than 25,000 votes in DeSoto County, significantly underperforming Trump. The last time she was on the ballot, in the presidential election year of 2020, Hyde-Smith performed as well as Trump in DeSoto County, winning more than 40,000 votes.
Put simply, if she had performed as well this year as she did in 2020 in that one county – DeSoto – she would not be staring at a potential history-making upset.
If he does win, Colom would be the first Democrat in Mississippi to win a U.S. Senate race since 1982 and the first challenger to upset an incumbent Mississippi senator since, gulp, 1942.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party at the Ice House in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
A long-running joke is the political prognosticator proclaiming to a spellbound audience that the outcome of the election would depend on turnout. All election outcomes depend on turnout.
But Tuesday’s Senate election in Mississippi really, no really, depended on turnout, and Scott Colom and his team should be credited for a campaign that turned out his voters for what could be one of the most improbable victories in the history of not only the state but the nation. Hyde-Smith was not able to turn out her voters at the same level.
It is no secret that midterm election turnout is generally much less than the turnout in presidential elections. The turnout for this year’s midterm in Mississippi is most likely record-breaking, nearing 1 million votes, but still more than 200,000 short of the turnout in the 2024 presidential election and more than 300,000 short of the total in the 2020 election.
The midterm turnout will be about 100,000 more than the 2023 Mississippi gubernatorial election in which incumbent Republican Tate Reeves beat Democrat Brandon Presley by about 25,000 votes.
DeSoto County provides the example of how Colom was able to exceed Presley’s performance. Colom got nearly 15,000 more votes than Presley in the county.
DeSoto is not the only reason for Colom’s stunningly strong performance, but it is the biggest factor.
And it should be noted that DeSoto County has long been a bit of an enigma when it comes to Mississippi electioneering.
DeSoto for years has been the fastest or one of the fastest-growing Mississippi counties, thanks in large part to Memphis transplants. While the county grew to one of the state’s largest, it also was home to a large number of low-propensity voters. The Tennessee transplants did not appear to take much of an interest in Mississippi elections.
In 1999, Ronnie Musgrove, Mississippi’s last Democratic governor, barely lost to Republican Mike Parker in DeSoto County by a vote of 9,301 to 9,144. But in 2003, Musgrove’s Republican challenger, Haley Barbour, recognized the potential of DeSoto County and spent an inordinate amount of time campaigning in the Memphis suburb. Then-President George W. Bush campaigned for Barbour in DeSoto County. Barbour’s work led to him defeating Musgrove in DeSoto by 18,689 votes to 8,876 votes.
With that performance, DeSoto was birthed as one of the state’s  Republican strongholds.
Trump captured more than 60% of the votes in DeSoto County in each of his three presidential campaigns and a high of 48,064 votes in 2024. Remember, Hyde-Smith won fewer than 25,000 votes there last week.
Outside of presidential elections, though, DeSoto countians still appear to have only a lukewarm interest in Mississippi elections and politicians.
That is most likely why Trump came to DeSoto in 2018 during Hyde-Smith’s initial Senate campaign to stump for her.
This year, Trump opted to go to Corinth in northeast Mississippi instead of DeSoto County on the northwest side of the  state to campaign for Hyde-Smith.
Perhaps that decision was the wrong one. Or perhaps, Trump’s policies are unpopular even in what is believed to be a Republican stronghold like DeSoto County.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s Sen. Bernie Sanders poised to get back powerful committee chair in new Congress
description:
He wants the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee to “be very aggressive about moving toward ‘Medicare for All’” and restore the healthcare subsidies Congress allowed to lapse last year.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s Sen. Bernie Sanders poised to get back powerful committee chair in new Congress.
text:
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, speaks during a press conference with U.S. Senator Peter Welch, D-Vermont, at the Statehouse in Montpelier in February 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
After Tuesday’s election swept Democrats into control of both houses of Congress, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said he intends to get back the powerful post he held two years ago: chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.
He’ll use that post, he said in an interview, to try to rescind provisions in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act that are slated to push millions of people off Medicaid and to restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that helped many people afford health insurance before Congress allowed the subsidies to lapse last year. 
Sanders also wants the committee to “be very aggressive about moving toward ‘Medicare for All,’” he said Thursday. “We’re going to move to do what every other major country does: guarantee healthcare to all people as a human right.”
Sanders’ post would likely be the most high-profile example of the expanded power the three members of Vermont’s congressional delegation will enjoy when a new Congress is seated in January. As of Friday afternoon, Democrats — with whom Sanders caucuses — were projected to control at least 54 seats in the Senate and 253 in the House, according to The Associated Press, though some races still hadn’t been called. The election has been widely viewed as a rebuke of Trump and the Republican Party. 
Sanders said he also wants to advance legislation called the PRO Act that would make it easier for workers to join a union and bargain collectively with their employer. The bill passed the House in 2020 and again in 2021 but has repeatedly stalled in the Senate. 
He wants to pass a bill that would raise the federal minimum wage to $20 per hour, from the current $7.25, he said, as well as legislation that would raise taxes on billionaires to fund low- or no-cost early childhood education and daycare for families nationwide.  
Sanders had two major takeaways from the election: There is “growing revulsion and disgust with the behavior and the policies of the Trump administration,” he said, while people are also deeply worried about how to afford necessities like food and gas. Those rising costs are tied to Trump’s war in Iran, which Sanders said the new Congress needs to end along with “U.S. military aid to the extremist government in Israel.” 
The new Democratic-controlled Congress will need to be good, he said, at “walking and chewing bubblegum at the same time.” 
“Trump’s illegal and unconstitutional actions cannot be ignored. He has got to be held accountable. Period,” Sanders said. “But, on the other hand, if that’s all that we do, and we ignore the pain and anxiety that working families are experiencing all over this country, we will be a failed Congress. So, I think we have to do both.” 
That’s a sentiment shared by Vermont’s two other members of Congress. 
U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., said she plans to push for legislation that builds on the bipartisan housing law Congress enacted earlier this year without Trump’s signature. It included provisions to streamline projects’ environmental reviews, remove restrictions on manufactured home construction, boost access to small-dollar mortgages and limit the number of homes a private equity firm can own. Balint wants to see additional housing reforms designed for rural communities, like many in Vermont, she said. 
Congress also needs to prioritize taking on corporate consolidation across a wide array of industries, she said, including fertilizer production, grocery stores, ticketing platforms and even fire truck manufacturing. 
Balint mentioned the Iran war too and thinks “step one” to ending the conflict is removing Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth from office. Impeachment proceedings start in the House; Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said he’ll again introduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth as soon as Monday, unless the secretary resigns first. 
“I keep telling people, it’s a target-rich environment. We have to be disciplined,” Balint said.
Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., told VTDigger’s Vermont Conversation podcast last week that although Democrats are right to celebrate their sweeping gains in Congress, the vote “was not a big embrace of Democrats.” Instead, Welch said, “what Democrats have been given by the American people is an opportunity to earn their trust.”
Top priorities for the new Congress should be repealing Trump’s tariffs on goods from Canada and many other countries around the world, he said, as well as taking whatever steps it can to curb the president’s immigration enforcement tactics, which he called violent and cruel. 
Democrats should focus on governing rather than political retribution, Welch told podcast host David Goodman.   
“There will be corruption investigations,” Welch said. But accountability should be “about making life better for everyday people, not a focus on corruption that is about vengeance and payback.”
Olivia Gieger contributed reporting.

title: Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens’ CUSA championship aspirations are dashed with loss to Kennesaw State

text:
A picture of the pylon at Delaware Stadium during the Fightin’ Blue Hens first game of the 2026 season against Merrimack. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder.
The Kennesaw State Owls (3-6, 2-3 CUSA) defeated the Fightin’ Blue Hens (4-5, 2-3 CUSA), 42-40, on November 7, making the Blue Hens chance at a CUSA title improbable.
 
Delaware quarterback Nick Minicucci received the shotgun snap and took his drop while surveying the Kennesaw State defense. Minicucci kept his eyes downfield on fourth and six, but felt the Owl pass rush closing in. The Owl’s outside pass rushers forced Minicucci to step up in the pocket where their interior teammates awaited the senior’s arrival. 
Minicucci tried to navigate himself out of the pocket, but all the Owl pass rushers converged on him as he attempted to escape. Linebacker Tywon Christopher was the player to take him down, giving the ball back to the Kennesaw State offense with over four minutes to play in the third quarter.
Christopher’s third quarter sack was one of three sacks the Kennesaw defense accumulated throughout the game in the Owls’ 42-40 victory over UD, Saturday evening.
The Delaware offensive line struggled against the Kennesaw front seven throughout the night allowing the three sacks along with nine quarterback hurries. Minicucci seemed like he was scrambling on many of his dropbacks and the running game never gained any momentum, rushing for 85 total yards. 
Despite the struggles up front, UD still had a chance to come away with a win. 
Following the turnover on downs, Conference USA (CUSA) interception leader, George Mullins, picked off Owl quarterback Landon Varnes and returned it into Owl territory. The interception led to a Tucker Smack field goal that put the Blue Hens ahead, 34-33, near the end of the third quarter.
Varnes and the Kennesaw offense immediately bounced back, scoring 42 seconds into the fourth quarter on a 63-yard touchdown pass to Reed Jesiolowski. Jesiolowski was wide open running down the numbers on the left side of the field behind the Delaware secondary when Varnes hit him in stride for the long touchdown. The Owls attempted a two-point conversion, but the try was intercepted by Blue Hen defensive back Kevin Moore. 
A Delaware punt followed the Kennesaw State scoring drive and the Owls added a field goal on their next possession, increasing their advantage to eight with 8:25 left to play. 
Delaware’s offense continued to struggle after the field goal and ended their next two drives with a lost fumble and punt. The Blue Hen defense made key stops down the stretch and forced the Owls to punt the ball away late in the fourth quarter. The Delaware defense gave the offense one last shot to tie the game with a minute and 47 seconds remaining and 82 yards of field to traverse. 
Delaware’s offense capitalized on the opportunity and marched down the field to the Kennesaw State 17 yard line with thirty seconds remaining in the game. Minicucci attempted a pass on first down, but the throw was hurried and fell incomplete. Delaware’s signal caller attempted a second pass on second down and connected with receiver Bryson Graves running across the middle of the field. Graves out ran the Owl defense and crossed into the endzone with 24 seconds remaining in the game.

BRYSON GRAVES  pic.twitter.com/qp0TEYZezv
— Delaware Football (@Delaware_FB) November 7, 2026

The Blue Hens lined up for the two-point conversion and schemed up a play that seemed designed for Graves to sneak out into the left flat out of a condensed formation. Graves slipped as he started his route and Minicucci quickly pivoted his focus from Graves to the Owl pass rush bearing down on him. Minicucci scrambled to his right and threw on the run to Donovan Lewis in the back right of the endzone. Lewis made a diving effort for the throw, but was unable to come up with the catch.
Delaware’s onside kick attempt was recovered by the Owls and Kennesaw State went into victory formation to secure the win. 
The Blue Hens finished the game with 493 total yards of offense with 408 of those yards coming from the passing game. Minicucci finished with 35 completions on 54 attempts and two throwing touchdowns putting him two away from second place on Delaware’s all-time passing touchdowns list. Graves finished the game with a team-high seven catches and 125 receiving yards (both are career highs) notching his first career game of over 100 receiving yards. Jo Silver led the running back room with 39 yards on the ground. 
The Owls offense finished with similar totals with 446 total yards, 309 of which through the air. Kennesaw State did out rush the Blue Hens, 137 to 85, accumulating 107 of those rush yards in the second quarter. 
The Owls scored 17 points in the second quarter with both of their touchdowns coming via the run game and running back Boogie Woods III. Woods finished the game with 90 rushing yards on 15 carries to go along with the two scores. 
Blue Hen running back Viron Ellison Jr. also finished the first half with a pair of touchdowns, scoring one in the first quarter and his second in the second quarter.  
The first quarter got off to an explosive start after the Owls scored in the first 20 seconds of action. Redshirt senior Davis Bryson fielded the game’s opening kick-off and found a hole near the left side of Delaware’s kick coverage. Bryson took advantage of the opening and streaked down the left sideline passing the lone defender in his way, kicker Tucker Smack, en route to a 99-yard return touchdown. 
The Blue Hens answered with a methodical drive that lasted nearly seven minutes and ended with the first of Ellison’s two touchdowns. The Delaware defense followed with defensive tackle Trace Scott III’s first career interception and touchdown, giving the Blue Hens a 15-6 lead with a little less than seven minutes to play in the quarter.

Pick six  pic.twitter.com/cw34QGpFEz
— Delaware Football (@Delaware_FB) November 7, 2026

The Owls bounced back from the turnover and cut the lead to two with a drive that ended in a Rickie Collins eight-yard touchdown run along the right sideline. Originally called out of bounds before the score, the play was reviewed and deemed a touchdown due to Collins’ ability to reach the ball out past the pylon as his body was pushed out of bounds. 
That was the last snap Collins played in the game. Collins was on the sideline with ice on his right shoulder and his pads off when the Owls’ offense took the field at the start of the second quarter. Junior Landon Varnes took over under center and played the rest of the game finishing with 254 passing yards and a quarterback rating of 112.5.
The Owls’ win keeps them in the hunt for a bowl game with their overall record sitting at 3-6 with three games remaining on their schedule. 
The Blue Hens’ loss makes it very improbable they end the season with a chance at the CUSA title. 
Delaware sits behind Jacksonville State, Liberty, Middle Tennessee and is tied with New Mexico State in the CUSA standings. Delaware has already lost to Liberty and Middle Tennessee this season and will play New Mexico State and Jax State within the next three weeks. The Blue Hens would need to win out and hope for a pair of losses from Middle Tennessee and three straight losses from Jax State to have a shot at playing in the CUSA championship game.
Delaware is also a couple wins away from being bowl eligible. The Blue Hens will need to win two of their next three games to play in their second bowl game in just their second season at the FBS level. 
The Blue Hens’ next game is against FIU at home on Saturday, November 14. Kick-off will be at 3:00 p.m.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Data shows little change in CT housing voucher segregation
description: Advocates say the Section-8 system has led to significant housing segregation, where most voucher holders have to live in cheaper areas.
text:
Until about a decade ago, people living in Bridgeport and Fairfield got the same amount of money for their housing vouchers, even though rent is much higher in Fairfield.
The amount of aid through the federally-funded housing choice voucher program — better known as Section 8 — is determined by averaging rent costs in a large, economically diverse metro area.
These housing vouchers, used at private apartments, are typically administered through towns and can be used anywhere in a set region. But using such a big geographic area to determine the voucher value made it hard for people to live in wealthier towns like Fairfield. Because of this, advocates say the widely used system led to significant housing segregation, with most voucher holders forced to live in lower-income areas with cheaper rents because it’s all they can afford. 
“That means you’re actually kind of coming up with a number that is going to be too low to ever reach a lot of places that are higher-rent areas,” Erin Boggs, executive director of Open Communities Alliance. 
To address this problem, federal rules were changed around 2017 to allow housing authorities to calculate voucher values based on ZIP code instead. But, since then, only two Connecticut authorities — Fairfield and Stratford — have opted to participate.
“It made a huge impact at least in Fairfield about the segregation that was really going on,” said Carol Martin, executive director of the Fairfield Housing Authority. “And when I say segregation, [it was] not intended by the rental assistance program. It was really driven by the markets.”
The areas with lower rents are often racially and economically segregated with lower-performing schools, more pollution and less access to outdoor space. A May 2026 report from the Open Communities Alliance found that around 50% of voucher holders in Connecticut lived in high poverty census tracts — and a Connecticut Mirror analysis of vouchers distributed in 2026 by ZIP code elicited similar outcomes.
The report attributed this segregation to voucher value and administrative barriers, among other issues. 
While housing authorities can opt-in to small area fair market rents, only the Hartford metro area is required to utilize it. And Boggs believes state law can be used to make this method of calculation the standard and begin to address this segregation.
“The state housing authorities are a creature of state law, right? So the state gets to say a lot about, certainly their jurisdiction,” Boggs said. “When they’re based on a concern about segregation, they can make rules that correct for that, like adopting these other versions of the value vouchers.”
Housing Committee co-Chair Sen. Martha Marx, D-New London, said she’d be interested in looking at ways to require towns to use the small area method to calculate voucher values.
“I think you almost have to make mandates, right?” Marx said. “Everybody hates mandates, but there’s a reason for mandates.” 
Housing Committee ranking member Rep. Tony Scott, R-Monroe, said he’d rather see mandates on the Department of Housing to use rental assistance in suburbs than mandates on towns. For its part, DOH officials say they do have housing mobility programs and other methods to reduce segregation.
“It alleviates the quote-unquote segregation,” Scott said. “It alleviates going to bad schools, alleviates that people all live together in bad crime areas. It alleviates all that. Let’s make it a priority for the DOH to say this is how we want to do these vouchers.”
The House and Senate Republican caucuses have historically opposed Democratic proposals to implement mandates on towns, particularly around housing. But with the midterm election resulting in a smaller GOP presence in the General Assembly, the question now turns to what housing priorities the state’s Democrats will set once the legislative session starts in January. 
Neighborhood rent
While she can’t remember the exact year the Fairfield Housing Authority started calculating voucher values by ZIP code, Martin said they opted in as soon as they could. The 2017 federal rule change made it possible for authorities to volunteer to switch their valuation systems and required some larger authorities to do so.
“[This] honestly was a huge success for Fairfield, because I think we’re a community that was uniquely positioned for the HUD to implement small area fair market rents,” Martin said. “It really put us into a much more sustainable program, and we availed ourselves of it almost as quickly as it became law.”
The hyperlocal method of voucher calculation was optional for Fairfield, but Martin knew it would benefit the area.
Under the old regulations, we were going to the highest percentage above fair market rent that we could through a normal regulation process. And we were still [on average] $300 less than what typical landlords were renting apartments to.Carol Martin, executive director of the Fairfield Housing Authority
Fairfield is grouped into the Bridgeport Regional Metro area, which includes towns like Trumbull, Bridgeport and Stratford. But Bridgeport has a median gross rent of $1,450 compared to $2,185 in Fairfield, and the median household income in Bridgeport is $113,747 less than it is in Fairfield. No one with a voucher has to pay more than a third of their income to rent; the amount each household receives changes based on income.
Because voucher value was calculated using the fair market rent for the region, Martin said, the Fairfield Housing Authority was “maxing out” their vouchers.
“Under the old regulations, we were going to the highest percentage above fair market rent that we could through a normal regulation process,” Martin said. “And we were still [on average] $300 less than what typical landlords were renting apartments to.”
Even with the flexibility to increase voucher value by 10%, Fairfield vouchers were not meeting rent costs in the area.
“Simply, the math didn’t work,” Martin said.
But this didn’t just mean that the vouchers were unusable — it meant that Fairfield was losing vouchers. After a certain point, they were given to a different housing authority.
“[Carol] was finding that her program was shrinking because this regional way of calculating the value of vouchers meant there was no way people could come up to the level of the rent in Fairfield,” Boggs said. “As soon as she adopted this, she was able to grow her program back.”
A CT Mirror analysis found that economic voucher segregation has not changed much over time. However, areas that have implemented the ZIP-code calculated rents have seen the percentage of voucher holders in high-poverty areas — those with poverty rates of 20% or higher — fall slightly since implementation. 
In 2017, under former President Barack Obama’s administration, larger housing authorities across the country were required to switch to the small area method of calculating rent.
The Hartford Metropolitan Statistical Area was among those that had to switch. Data shows the area has seen an increase in the number of voucher holders living outside high poverty areas over the past 12 years.
Since 2013, the number of voucher holders living in West Hartford increased, while the number of voucher holders living in Hartford, a high-poverty area, fell by almost four percentage points.
“When you look at the Hartford region, I think the combination between the mobility counseling and the small area FMR is helpful because they go hand in glove,” Steve DiLella, the director of the individual and family support programs at the Connecticut Department of Housing, said.
Mobility counseling, which helps families in higher-poverty cities areas relocate to different areas using their vouchers, is used by the state in Hartford, Middletown, Meriden, Fairfield, New Haven and Bridgeport, DiLella said. These programs help them identify places to live, aid in negotiation with landlords and provide help with financial management and tenant rights education.
New Haven — a high-poverty city — and New Milford both saw drops in both total count and percentage of voucher holders living in the towns since 2013. DiLella thinks mobility counseling, small area fair market rents, and the waitlist lottery system, which does not use jurisdiction to determine who gets the next available state voucher, all impact where voucher holders live.
Despite the decrease of vouchers seen in some high-poverty towns, the overall distribution of vouchers across the state remained fairly stagnant. There were 6,226 state-distributed housing choice vouchers in 2013 compared to 8,177 in 2025 due to an increase in federally funded specialty voucher programs during the pandemic and for veterans. But even with more vouchers, there was little change in where most people lived across the state.  
In 2013, 54.4% of state voucher holders lived in high poverty towns compared to 42.7% in 2025, CT Mirror’s analysis found. Around 3,390 vouchers were used in high poverty towns in 2013, compared to 3,494 in 2025. The OCA report also elicited similar results.
“The voucher programs, as originally envisioned, would have broken up that system so that people could live anywhere,” Hugh Bailey, policy director at Open Communities Alliance, said. “Part of what we’re trying to show is that, despite the promise and the potential of the voucher program, the outcome hasn’t really changed all that much.”
Hamden, Norwalk, New London, Stamford and Winchester saw the largest increases in percentage of total vouchers distributed year to year. DiLella said New London’s increase may be attributed to state vouchers given to folks who had previously been in public housing that closed. After public housing closed in the city, the state issued more project-based Section 8 housing, meaning that people got vouchers for specific apartment complexes. Towns like Hamden, meanwhile, may have seen an increase in voucher holders as a result of mobility counseling in nearby New Haven.
“Even when we do [mobility counseling], some households still choose to live in the community that may be in the cities,” DiLella said. “There is this piece of choice that I think sometimes in this conversation doesn’t always get recognized that, ultimately, even though we provide this level of service, households still can choose where they want, of their own free will.”
Historical segregation
Connecticut has a history of being one of the most economically and racially segregated states in the nation. A study released this year found that Connecticut schools are some of the most segregated in the nation, and a 2024 housing and segregation study found similar results.
A 2015 study from the Connecticut Fair Housing Center and the Connecticut Department of Housing detailed historic policies such as redlining and exclusionary zoning that fostered segregation and limited where families of color were permitted to live in the state. 
Housing decisions by the family are influenced by many factors, including schools, employment, transportation, healthcare, childcare, and family support systems. Every family has different priorities, and housing assistance should support those choices.Annette Sanderson, chief executive officer of Hartford housing authority
These policies, the study found, were still impacting housing segregation in the state.
“Connecticut’s fairly obviously racially and economically segregated, right, and whether it’s the worst, the third worst, the fifth worst [in the nation], I don’t really think is relevant to the conversation,” Sean Ghio, policy director for the Partnership for Strong Communities, said. “What are the outcomes for Connecticut because we continue to tolerate it?”
Annette Sanderson, chief executive officer of the Hartford housing authority, said in an emailed statement that when the agency made the switch to a small area rent calculation it was challenging to explain how vouchers used in different areas might be worth different amounts. Since implementation, there has been more flexibility for families who are looking for housing across the region.
“Housing decisions by the family are influenced by many factors, including schools, employment, transportation, healthcare, childcare, and family support systems,” Sanderson said. “Every family has different priorities, and housing assistance should support those choices.”
But not everyone wants to implement the calculation. In fact, some housing authorities are against making the switch.
“You hear two responses from housing authorities,” Boggs said. “One is, ‘These other areas cost more, so I’m going to have to give out more vouchers.'”
But Boggs said studies done by HUD found that housing authorities generally do not spend more money on vouchers under this calculation. Because fair market rent also inflates the cost of vouchers in areas with lower rents, the amount of money spent per voucher evens out.
However, Boggs also said local housing authorities cite administrative costs and the burden that switching over to a different calculation method would put on the housing authority.
Martin said the “upfront costs” to transition from fair market rents to small area fair market rents can be costly for a housing authority.
But once Fairfield made the switch, Martin said the program costs remained the same as before.
Homes in the southern part of the Barry Square neighborhood, part of Hartford’s 06114 zip code, are seen on Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Connecticut law
While only the Hartford metro area is required to use the small area fair market rents and other housing authorities can currently opt-in, Boggs said she believes state law can be used to make this method of calculation the standard.
“The state housing authorities are a creature of state law, right? So the state gets to say a lot about, certainly their jurisdiction,” Boggs said. “When they’re based on a concern about segregation, they can make rules that correct for that, like adopting these other versions of the value vouchers.”
The issue is complicated by several political realities around housing policy in Connecticut. It’s hard to get significant housing legislation passed, particularly if it includes mandates for towns. Some Republicans also view vouchers as a way to help their smaller towns get closer to a 10% affordable housing threshold under a state law known as 8-30g, one of the state’s foremost affordable housing laws. Democrats want to push those towns to build more housing to meet the threshold instead.
Marx said she views the issue as one of public health. The Open Communities Alliance  report notes that many low-income families have environmentally-driven health issues and want to move to a place with less pollutants.
“It’s almost not a voucher issue; it’s a public health issue. It is just so sad that life is already so hard for people, and we are just giving them no choice,” Marx said.
But, she added, there are several priorities for Democrats in the upcoming legislative session. Eviction reform has been an area of focus for committee leadership over the past few years, and Marx said she wants to look at changing minimum lot sizes statewide.
Housing Committee co-Chair Rep. Antonio Felipe, D-Bridgeport, said homelessness is his priority for the coming session. He said he’d be interested in talking about voucher segregation, but fears that increasing voucher values could mean fewer vouchers overall.
He wants to focus on getting rent costs down across the board, he said.
“I think it’s super important that we figure out a way to tackle segregation overall. That we figure out a way to make communities like Bridgeport and Fairfield — which are so different but neighbor each other — work together in terms of making sure that we are providing good and affordable housing for people,” Felipe said.
Connecticut Republicans have long sought a way to reform the 8-30g statute. The law offers court remedies to developers whose affordable housing proposals are denied, shifting the burden of proof to the town to show it had legitimate health or safety issues.
Towns are exempt from the law if at least 10% of their housing stock is designated affordable. One of the ways to increase that stock is by having housing choice vouchers in the community. In 2025, Scott, the Republican state representative from Monroe, backed a proposal that would have prioritized voucher use in towns that haven’t hit that 10% threshold.
He said he sees that as one of the ways to address segregation concerns and help towns make easier progress toward the 10% goal.
“It’s not going to be like building a 100-unit complex with 30 of them being affordable housing, but it will help,” Scott said. His bill didn’t get a public hearing in 2025.
Democrats and housing advocates have been reluctant to make changes to 8-30g, saying it’s one of few tools available to push towns that refuse to allow construction to do their part in alleviating the affordable housing crisis.
“They’re doing that just as a way to get out of building” new housing, Marx said.
But Housing Committee ranking member Sen. Rob Sampson, R-Wolcott, one of three state senators who won his reelection campaign this week, said he fundamentally disagrees with the idea of the government intervening to change the demographic makeup of any community. He said he wants to see people who really need vouchers get them but thinks too many people take advantage of the program.
“I think that they are being disadvantaged by these programs being available,” Sampson said. “They end up as a crutch instead of people becoming more self-starting and entrepreneurial.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: It’s the morning after a historic election reshaped American politics. What comes next is crucial.
description: What’s next? There are few things more stirring than the Kansas sky at dawn, and the election results on the morning of Nov. 4 rolled like thunder across the prairie. We are less than a week out from that historic election, in which a Democrat from the Sunflower State was elected to the U.S. Senate […]
text:
Dawn breaks on Oct. 19, 2026, over Emporia, Kansas. (Photo by Kim Horner McCoy)What’s next?
There are few things more stirring than the Kansas sky at dawn, and the election results on the morning of Nov. 4 rolled like thunder across the prairie. We are less than a week out from that historic election, in which a Democrat from the Sunflower State was elected to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1932, and many of us are still basking in the promise of a new political day.
The short list of upheavals: Both houses of Congress were resoundingly wrenched from GOP control in a stunning rebuke to the administration of President Donald Trump. Kansas Republicans lost their supermajority in the Kansas House, effectively ending their single-party ability to override the governor’s veto. Democrats won the majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years, and Kansan Cindy Holscher will likely join them, pending results of a close-race audit.
Pundits will dissect the 2026 midterm for years to come, but I doubt their analyses will add much to what we already know, that the spectacular unpopularity of Trump and his corrupt and inhumane actions drove us to the polls with a renewed sense of purpose.
The economy was killing us, as anybody who’s pumped gas or bought groceries in the last six months knows, but affordability wasn’t the only reason most of us voted for change. What we shared was a collective sense of moral outrage over a clumsy and ill-advised war with Iran, a deadly and sadistic immigration policy, a federal government so rife with corruption it resembles organized crime, and the incoherent blustering and brazen indecency of Trump himself. We longed for a return to decency, competence in government, and the progressive ideals that had shaped America since the end of World War II.
Not all of us voted alike, I know.
But when I use the collective I’m speaking for the majority of voters, in Kansas and across the nation, who came together in the unlikeliest of circumstances. It is rare that I’m able to claim part in a majority, but the fact that I can now is a testament to why political analyst Charlie Cook called the midterm a “unicorn election” in rural America.
Now that the unicorn has been verified as an uncommon but real part of the political taxonomy of the nation, it is time to survey the terrain. There are two years remaining in Trump’s second term, the Supreme Court is largely sympathetic to him, and there are still two months to wait before the new Congress is sworn in.
So, what’s next?
The danger is that this new era will be shaped by what it opposes instead of what it hopes to achieve.
Coming together to fight a common threat to democracy is a noble thing. Without that kind of collective effort, no would-be authoritarian would ever be stopped. But now the election is over, it is not enough simply to resist Trump’s vision of America.
We must have our own vision.
And that takes leadership.
If somebody presses me to define leadership, I’m likely to say, “I know it when I see it,” a joke that references Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart’s 1964 remark about pornography. I’m likely to make a joke of it because whenever anybody starts using the word “leadership,” they’re often talking about themselves, and that makes me nervous. None of the best leaders I know ever refer to themselves in that way, or wrote a book about leadership or gave inspirational seminars in how to be a leader.
They just led.
There is a thread connecting the best leaders in American history, a durable but winding political sinew that stretches back to the founding of the country. That sinew is the effort to advance, in equality and prosperity and the pursuit of happiness, the human condition. For all of us. I’ve talked about some of these leaders in my columns before, especially Abraham Lincoln and Dwight Eisenhower. In retrospect, fighting slavery or battling fascism might seem like simple choices, but few choices are uncomplicated in the fever of current events.
Consider Teddy Roosevelt, who came to Kansas in 1910 to talk about the “New Nationalism.” In a speech at Osawatomie, the former president, a Republican, mentioned Lincoln often as he addressed a crowd filled with Union veterans of the Civil War. Roosevelt urged better wages for workers and the end of government protections for businesses.
“At many stages in the advance of humanity, this conflict between the men who possess more than they have earned and the men who have earned more than they possess is the central condition of progress,” Roosevelt said.
Roosevelt advocated an eight-hour workday, a minimum wage for women, insurance for the unemployed and the elderly, and a bracketed income tax. Roosevelt’s Progressive Party lost, but the ideas stuck.
In 2011, President Barrack Obama, a Democrat, went to Osawatomie. At a speech at the high school there, he picked up the plea for the middle class that Roosevelt had made a century before.
“This is the defining issue of our time,” Obama said. “This is a make-or-break moment for the middle class, for all those who are fighting to get into the middle class. Because what’s at stake is whether this will be a country where working people can earn enough to raise a family, build a modest savings, own a home, secure their retirement.”
Obama was speaking just a few years after the Great Recession, the longest and deepest economic slump in 70 years. Obama noted that for his “New Nationalism” speech, Roosevelt was called a socialist and even a communist. But the same things that Roosevelt railed against in 1910 were still problems in 2011.
Inequality, he said, distorts democracy.
“It gives an outsized voice to the few who can afford high-priced lobbyists and unlimited campaign contributions,” Obama said, “and it runs the risk of selling out our democracy to the highest bidder.”
Fifteen years after Obama gave that speech, the rich have stadium-sized PA systems while the rest of us whisper.
Elon Musk, the richest man in the world, gave more in political contributions for the 2026 midterms than any other donor in American history, according to an analysis by the New York Times. That superlative in spending is for a non-candidate contributor in a single election cycle. Musk’s disclosed political donations to state and federal political groups amounted to $474 million since Jan. 1, 2025. Those contributions went to Republican-aligned PACs, and half of it was spent in Texas, where Musk has a Tesla factory and launches his SpaceX rockets.
Musk must have been particularly frustrated by last week’s election, because Texas elected Democrats to the U.S. Senate and all statewide offices.
But the fact that a single individual can pump half a billion dollars into an American election in an attempt to influence the outcome should be a source of national outrage. Such lavish giving was made possible by the 2010 Citizens United Supreme Court decision, which ended longstanding restrictions on outside political contributions.
That Musk’s millions made little difference in the midterms seems a civic miracle, or at least a testament to the power of whispers when combined. Personally, I haven’t been able to stand the sight of those wedge-shaped stainless steel Tesla trucks since he wielded the DOGE chainsaw at the Conservative Political Action Conference last year.
It was an absurd act, a bit of political theater about slashing bureaucracy, but it had something that other MAGA antics didn’t. It was memorable. I suspect that in time the chainsaw burlesque will come to symbolize the clownishness and danger of the second Trump administration.
While the midterms seem to have dealt the MAGA movement a crippling if not fatal blow, as Trump has become politically radioactive, they have also introduced uncertainty into the Democratic Party.
With big wins should come big change.
The old Democratic leadership — Chuck Schumer in the Senate, for example — might not suit a party renewed by a historic victory. If the symbol of MAGA is a chainsaw, then the symbol of the Democratic Party during the Trump era is a sternly worded letter.
Schumer, who is 76, seems too timid for the task ahead.
Articulating a new vision for America while holding Trump and his administration to account will require not just confidence, but boldness. That the Democratic Party failed so badly in 2024 by allowing Trump a second term is reason enough to take a hard look at the established leadership. Schumer ought to be asking his imaginary typical middle-class couple on Long Island, Joe and Eileen Bailey, about whether it’s time for him to step aside. Since they’re fictional, I can answer for them.
The answer is yes.
The question is not just who is bold enough to lead us out of the Trump era, but who has the courage and vision to help us escape a trajectory that has eroded American democracy and deepened inequality for decades.
“The historic nature of this election cannot be overstated,” observed historian Heather Cox Richardson the day after. “It is a rejection of Trump, who insisted voters should imagine he was on the ballot. But more than that, it is a rejection of the Republican ideology that has driven American politics since the 1980s: the idea that some people are better than others and have the right to rule.”
Our current system of checks on presidential power was the result of reforms instituted by Congress in the 1970s after the abuses of Richard Nixon infuriated the nation. But a docile GOP-controlled Congress has failed to use the tools available in Trump’s second term, even though Trump’s offenses are legion.
When the new Congress is sworn in, on Jan. 3, 2027, it will be up to them to use those tools, including the War Powers and Ethics in Government acts. It will also be necessary to create new laws to prevent the kind of chaos and corruption that has marked the Trump era. In addition, there will be a dizzying array of challenges facing lawmakers, topped by ending the war with Iran, bringing down prices for food and fuel and curbing ICE.
In addition, and perhaps most crucially, these things must be accomplished in a competent and even-handed manner, with no hint of retribution but with a full commitment to accountability. This might mean impeachment, but in the service of justice and not revenge.
Our new Congress must not only demonstrate good judgment and a fealty to law; it must not simply articulate an enthusiastic and humane vision of the future; and it must not merely be satisfied with the partisan divisions of the past. It must repair a government while healing a nation. It must act, not merely for the good of any one party, but for the benefit of all.
As Roosevelt said in Osawatomie:
“The object of government is the welfare of the people. The material progress and prosperity of a nation are desirable chiefly so long as they lead to the moral and material welfare of all good citizens.”
Leadership isn’t about power, but about the wise use of power.
So, what’s next?
Readers will recognize that I have borrowed this phrase from Aaron Sorkin’s television series, “The West Wing,” which ran for seven seasons, ending in 2006. In it, Martin Sheen plays fictional Democratic president Jed Bartlet, whose signature phrase, after one problem was solved, was “what’s next?”
The Sorkin series is fictional, but it is also aspirational. It articulates a vision of how government should work on behalf of average Americans. Much of it is about the use and abuses of power.
The Democratic Party has an opportunity to begin the rebuilding of government on competence and compassion. What’s next is what is now unexpectedly in reach. In addition to the obligation to repair democracy’s foundation is the chance to work for those things that most Americans want and desperately need. That includes universal healthcare, protecting Social Security, and shoring up voting and other constitutional rights. It means providing meaningful protections to vulnerable populations among us, especially the poor and migrants and those who peacefully live or love differently. Finally, it is an opportunity to renew America’s global commitment to freedom by defending our allies, honoring our promises and promoting democracy abroad.
So, what’s next?
It’s the promise of America.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT transit: The good, bad and unfinished
description: How many promises have we been given about fixing Connecticut's  transportation woes? How many have been kept? I checked.
text:
How many promises have we been given about fixing our state’s transportation woes?  How many press conferences have been held, initiatives launched and million dollar studies conducted… and for what benefit?
I engaged a little help from AI to start my research and generate a complete scorecard which you can access here. 



The good news:
There is a new train station in Windsor Locks  and another one is being built for Enfield (only 26 years after first being recommended).  Naugatuck too will get a new station as the Waterbury line remains closed (until May of ’27) for major upgrades.  Enjoy those bustitutes.
Renovations are underway for the interior of the beautiful Union Station in New Haven (complete with a new bar!).  A massive roof-like train shed for the track area is still just an unfunded drawing, but a pretty one at that.

A rendering of the new Enfield train station under construction. Credit: CTgov.com

About $340 million is to be spent over nine years upgrading three miles of track between Bridgeport and Stratford.  Do the math:  that’s $113 million a mile.  Total budget for the New Haven line speed enhancements, $1.6 billion over nine years.
The Special Transportation Fund is projected to end FY2027 with a $209 million surplus… in the same year as two fare hikes.
Sixty new railcars from Alstom should start arriving for testing late this year.
Ridership on Metro-North is back to about 90% of pre-COVID levels, with weekends well above those numbers.  And on-time performance is running close to 98%, helped by padded schedules.
The bad news:
Service (and ridership) on Shore Line East has still not been revived to pre-2020 numbers.  Unwilling to pay Amtrak to use its overhead wires and power, the Connecticut Department of Transportation returns to diesel locomotives on what had been all-electric service.  Shoreline commuters can enjoy the nostalgia.  And the fumes.
Commuter rail fares in Connecticut went up 10% in just 10 months. The state didn’t fully fund the trains, so now you can.
Amtrak and Metro-North are still at war.
Seven highway workers have been killed in six years, fixing our highways.  Tragic and avoidable. Slow down!
Work continues on the $1 billion Walk rail bridge replacement in Norwalk. The promised completion of 2029 is now stretched out to 2031.
And “Shapiro’s Folly” continues to metastasize, as its housing developer-turned-visionary is now adding a tunnel to his proposed $50 billion bridge crossing Long Island Sound.  Why talk about building one thing we can’t afford, when you can talk about building two?
The unfinished: 
This list is the longest as our memories are too short to keep up with all we’ve been promised over the years.
How many of us remember the 20-year plan to rebuild the Hartford viaduct on I-84, since shelved and rolled into yet another study?  Or the 20+ year effort to build an interchange between the Merritt Parkway and Route 7 in Norwalk, soon to be restarted in late ‘27?
Whatever happened to the study to electrify the Hartford, Waterbury and Danbury rail lines which was due in 2025?
Or the long-promised West Hartford train station on the Hartford line, now 30% designed and 0% funded?
And yes, who can ever forget Gov. Ned Lamont’s 2019 pledge known as “30-30-30”, promising a 30-minute ride from Hartford to New Haven (now 45 minutes, at best), 30 minutes from New Haven to Stamford (now 65 minutes on average) and 30 minutes from Stamford to New York City (now 58 minutes in peak hours)?
Our state loves to solve problems by “studying” them… over and over.  Studies, though costly, are cheaper than real solutions. Real fixes cost money which our lawmakers seem reluctant to find.
As one wag pointed out on social media “Goals are sold as accomplishments,” and so are more studies.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Lessons – and opportunities – from starter home ballot question loss
description: As Democrats across the country celebrated historic election victories as a mandate to tackle affordability, here in deep-blue Massachusetts voters rejected a tangible solution to one of the biggest drivers of our affordability crisis: housing costs.
text:
BY A RAZOR-THIN margin, Massachusetts voters rejected Question 7, the ballot measure that would have capped minimum lot size requirements for single-family homes at 5,000 square feet. 
This commonsense reform could have unlocked thousands of new homes. Estimates ranged from a conservative 750 a year to more than 5,000 a year. More importantly, it would have begun undoing decades of exclusionary zoning that encouraged McMansions and pushed starter homes toward extinction. 
Our chamber enthusiastically endorsed the measure, the first business association in Massachusetts to do so. We did so because we saw an opportunity to create homes for young professionals near their jobs or where they grew up. Homes for teachers and police officers in the towns they serve. Homes where seniors could downsize without leaving their neighborhoods. 
As Democrats across the country celebrated historic election victories as a mandate to tackle affordability, here in deep-blue Massachusetts voters rejected a tangible solution to one of the biggest drivers of our affordability crisis: housing costs.  
Instead, the status quo prevailed, with Question 7 defeated in the closest outcome of the record-tying nine ballot questions, with 50.6 percent of voters saying no versus 49.4 percent voting yes.  
Opposition came from different directions, driven by concerns about developer profits, changing “neighborhood character,” and the loss of local control. But with a margin this narrow, it helps to look at what tipped the balance and, more importantly, the silver lining we see in the results.  
Because after all, the housing crisis that is crushing our economy and dampening our young adults’ spirits remains.  
Those who voted ‘no’ didn’t know 
Question 7 was designed to be as inoffensive as possible. While the MBTA Communities Act required cities and towns — some unaccustomed to large apartment buildings — to zone for multifamily housing, Question 7 took almost the opposite approach. 
It would have opened the door to the very type of housing opponents to new growth often claim they want to preserve: single-family homes. Homes they, their parents, or grandparents owned. Homes now being bulldozed for McMansions. 
Here is an often under-explained, but crucial, detail of the ballot question: Question 7 applied only to properties with access to public water and sewer — effectively excluding more than 78 percent of Massachusetts’s land area. 
That should have reassured those in rural communities worried about infrastructure and development. Instead, the communities where the law wouldn’t have applied were among its strongest opponents.  

Municipalities with 90 percent to 100 percent sewer coverage supported Question 7 by more than 10 points. 


Municipalities with no sewer coverage, where the law would not have applied, rejected it by more than 20 points. 

In other words, many voters appear to have opposed changes they feared would come to their backyards, even though it would have had little or no impact in their neighborhoods or town. The places where Question 7 could have done the most good were generally supportive, while the places where it would have had little or no effect on local development helped defeat it. 
With a margin this small, that mattered. 
Political muscle was MIA 
Question 7 was conceived by Andrew Mikula, a long-time Wellesley housing advocate and chief housing economist at Pioneer Institute (he led this effort outside his day job). 
Mikula is a soft-spoken, thoughtful, clear-headed thinker. He tirelessly championed this effort and was its ever-present face, voice, and heart. He had support from the pro-housing advocacy group Abundant Housing Massachusetts, the Citizens’ Housing & Planning Association, Eastern Bank’s Bob Rivers, and others. 
Plus endorsements from the Globe, The New York Times, and even the Boston Herald. 
We have nothing but respect, admiration, and gratitude for Mikula’s efforts. But the yes campaign lacked the political muscle and pizzazz we saw, for example, last week in New York City. 
There, Mayor Zohran Mamdani championed a successful push for five ballot proposals aimed at streamlining government processes, cutting red tape, and accelerating development. 
Yes, Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll endorsed the measure. But they were understandably focused on their own reelection. 
Sen. Ed Markey was running too. He announced he was voting yes just days before the election, in a single social media post. Markey’s general election was a slam dunk; surely, he could have expended some political capital on this while crossing the state. 
And where was Sen. Elizabeth Warren? Her career has been all about lifting up the middle class. She shepherded bipartisan legislation to expand housing production this year. She’s made housing affordability a major focus of her work.   
Among the state’s congressional delegation, only Rep. Jake Auchincloss was an early champion of Question 7. And Rep. Bill Keating was the only other member of our delegation on the ballot committee’s list of official endorsers. 
With a margin this small, that mattered. 
Was the message just too wonky? 
Here’s something else we’ve been wrestling with: Did voters actually understand what Question 7 would do? 
Minimum lot sizes aren’t exactly intuitive. Explaining zoning requires striking a delicate balance. Too much technical detail loses voters. Too little leaves room for confusion and misinformation. 
The campaign, operating on a limited budget, struggled with that balance. Consider its sole television ad. The 30-second spot offered just one explanation: “Yes on Question 7 will help us build the homes we need.” 
True. But that was about it. And the dense, technical language voters encountered on their ballots probably didn’t help. 
Explaining that “smaller lots mean smaller houses, which can mean cheaper houses” would have been a good start. Helping people understand that 5,000 square feet is about the size of an NBA basketball court would have helped, too. 
So would positioning this as the alternative to “mansionization.” Nobody loves when a McMansion springs up in their neighborhood. It’s the one thing reflexive anti-development NIMBYs and YIMBYs (the acronym for pro-housing “yes in my backyard” advocates) both agree on. 
With a margin this small, this mattered. 
OK, so now what? 
Despite our disappointment, we see a silver lining. 
Voters in Brookline, Newton, Watertown, Arlington, Randolph, Amherst, Waltham, Malden, among others, backed this zoning change. 
Those results should send a message to their city and town halls, including those like Brookline and Newton, which in some areas require single-family lots up to eight times the size Question 7 would have allowed. (That’s nearly a football field, without the end zones.) 
Allowing 5,000-square-foot lots locally could help stem mansionization. It would create opportunities for smaller, more affordable homes in some of the state’s most expensive markets. Opportunities for folks to stay here. Opportunities for others to enjoy our special communities. Customers for our local businesses. 
We call on city councils and select boards in our suburban communities — and in communities across Massachusetts that supported Question 7 — to act. 
Finally, what about the state? 
The narrow defeat of this small, simple reform may tempt some Beacon Hill lawmakers to retreat from top-down state zoning reforms. But retreating doesn’t address our soul-crushing housing crisis. Courage does. 
Doing nothing is driving young adults out of state, leaving seniors stuck in homes they can’t maintain, and businesses struggling to attract and retain talent. 
Last week, more than 1.25 million Massachusetts voters said yes to Question 7. They said yes to loosening exclusionary zoning rules, even at the expense of some local control. That’s hardly a ringing endorsement of the status quo. 
We urge House and Senate lawmakers to approve two important proposals in the pending economic development bill: legislation to legalize duplexes statewide and so-called YIGBY legislation (“yes in God’s backyard”), which would make it easier for religious institutions to develop multifamily housing on their property. 
Then we need to keep pushing. Keep moving forward. Keep building. We need to act as if future generations are depending on us, because they are. 
With a crisis this large, this matters. 
Greg Reibman is president and CEO of the Charles River Regional Chamber. Max Woolf is the chamber’s public policy and government affairs manager. Reibman was one of the 10 original signers of the petition to place Question 7 on the ballot.

title: Salesianum and Newark Charter earn top seeds in the 2026 DIAA Boys Soccer State Tournaments
description: The 2026 DIAA Boys Soccer State Tournaments begin on November 10 with the first round of the division two state tournament. Salesianum earned the No. 1 seed in division one and Newark Charter earned the honor in division two.    Delaware high schools’ sports postseason is underway with the 2026 DIAA Field Hockey and Volleyball State Tournaments already in th[...]
text:
This image was generated using AI
The 2026 DIAA Boys Soccer State Tournaments begin on November 10 with the first round of the division two state tournament. Salesianum earned the No. 1 seed in division one and Newark Charter earned the honor in division two. 
 
Delaware high schools’ sports postseason is underway with the 2026 DIAA Field Hockey and Volleyball State Tournaments already in the midst of competition. Boys soccer is joining the postseason calendar with the division two tournament beginning on Tuesday, November 10.
The top-seed in the division two tournament is the Newark Charter Patriots who finished the season with a 14-0-1 overall record. The Patriots one tie this season came in their game against the Charter School of Wilmington Forces. The Forces earned the fifth seed in the division one tournament.  
Salesianum claimed the top spot in the division one tournament with a record of 13-2. The Sals two losses were against out-of-state opponents from Kentucky and New Jersey. Salesianum won the state championship last season and have finished as state champions or the runner-ups the last 13 seasons. 
The division two state tournament will start with a first round played on November 10 and then be followed by the quarterfinal round on November 14. The top four seeds in the division two tournament earn a first round bye. Those teams are: Newark Charter, Tower Hill, St. Mark’s and St. Andrew’s. They’ll play their first games in the quarterfinal round. The division one tournament opens with the quarterfinal round played on November 12. All eight teams will participate in the quarterfinal round. 
Here’s a look at the upcoming boys soccer postseason schedule:
Division One
Quarterfinals: (All games played on November 12)
Salesianum boys soccer posing with the state championship banner after winning the 2025 DIAA Division One State Tournament. Photo credit: Ryan Colasanti
No. 1 Salesianum vs No. 8 Caesar Rodney: Sallies and Caesar Rodney will play each other for the second time this season in their quarterfinal matchup. The Sals beat the Riders, 9-0, earlier this season with a pair of goals apiece from senior Sawyer Valle and juniors Bryan Perez-Herrera and Brady Esser. The quarterfinal will be played at Abessinio Stadium at 5:30 p.m.
No. 2 Cape Henlopen vs No. 7 Sussex Central: The Vikings enter the state tournament with a 12 game winning streak that includes a win over Sussex Central on November 3. Viking junior Brooks Whaley scored two goals in the win and sophomore goalkeeper Kasen Adams earned eight saves preserving the shutout. The quarterfinal rematch will be played at Cape Henlopen at 6:00 p.m.
No. 3 Appoquinimink vs No. 6 Middletown: The Jaguars and Cavaliers renew a rivalry that spans across all athletic programs in their quarterfinal game which will be played at Appoquinimink at 6:00 p.m. The two teams played each other during the regular season with the Jaguars winning a close game, 1-0.   
No. 4 Delcastle vs No. 5 Charter School of Wilmington: This the lone quarterfinal matchup in which the two teams didn’t play each other during the regular season. The Forces enter the contest winners of three straight, shutting out their opponent in each win. Delcastle begins the postseason on a five game winning streak earning four shutout victories in that stretch. The game will be played at Abessinio Stadium at 7:30 p.m.
Division Two
Round One: (All games played on November 10, at 6:00 p.m.)
No. 5 Caravel vs No. 12 Glasgow: The Buccaneers and Dragons play each other for the first time this season when they match up at Caravel on Tuesday. This is the Dragons first playoff game since 2018 and the Buccaneers first since making it to the semi-final round in 2024.
No. 6 Woodbridge vs No. 11 Brandywine: The Blue Raiders and Bulldogs will play each other for the first time this season in round one. Woodbridge enters the game winners of three of its last five games. Brandywine has won four of its last five. This game will be played at Woodbridge.
No. 7 Concord vs No. 10 Lake Forest: This a rematch of both teams’ first game of the season. The Raiders and Spartans finished that September 9 game with a 0-0 tie where both defensive and goalkeeping units performed well. The Raiders and Spartans have since finished the season with 9-4-2 records. This game will be played at Odyssey Charter. 
No. 8 Sussex Academy vs No. 9 Delmar: The Seahawks and Wildcats will meet for the second time this season when they play at Sussex Academy in the first round. The Seahawks won the regular season matchup, 4-0, in late September with help from a two goal performance from senior Dominic Catlett. Junior Bodhin Williams and freshman Anderson Martin-Chilel also scored in the game.
Quarterfinals: (All games played on November 14)
No. 1 Newark Charter vs Winner of No. 8 Sussex Academy/No. 9 Delmar: This game will be played at 7:00 p.m. at Newark Charter.
No. 2 Tower Hill vs Winner of No. 7 Concord/No. 10 Lake Forest: This game will be played at Tower Hill at 6:00 p.m.
St. Mark’s Spartans boy’s soccer team taking a picture with the division two state championship banner after winning the 2025 state championship. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
No. 3 St. Mark’s vs Winner of No. 6 Woodbridge/No. 11 Brandywine: This game will start at 6:00 p.m. and be played at St. Mark’s.
No. 4 St. Andrew’s vs Winner of No. 5 Caravel/No. 12 Glasgow: This game will be played at St. Andrew’s and begin at 1:00 p.m.
