name: Kansas Reflector
title: National health experts dissect election wins, effects on healthcare policy
description: TOPEKA — A national health expert expects Democrats to quickly move to reverse Medicaid cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to restore Affordable Care Act premium subsidies, which led to millions of people losing health insurance coverage.  “The size of this blue tsunami means huge expectations for Democrats, especially on healthcare […]
text:
Janice Martin says, "Thank you, Jesus," after the news broadcast announced Adam Hamilton's win at Cindy Holscher's watch party Nov. 3, 2026, in Lenexa. As Democrats claimed wins across the country, political anaylsts began to consider what the new landscape in Washington, D.C., might mean for healthcare policies. (Photo by Baya Burgess/ Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A national health expert expects Democrats to quickly move to reverse Medicaid cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to restore Affordable Care Act premium subsidies, which led to millions of people losing health insurance coverage. 
“The size of this blue tsunami means huge expectations for Democrats, especially on healthcare because this was very much a healthcare election,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a national nonpartisan healthcare policy institute, on a Thursday webinar during which KFF experts talked about what happens next after Tuesday’s election.
Healthcare was a key issue for Adam Hamilton, Kansas’ Democratic candidate and presumed winner of the U.S. Senate race against incumbent Republican Roger Marshall. 
The big question as election results are finalized is whether Democrats can meet high expectations set for addressing healthcare issues, Levitt said. 
Democrats will really only have the next year to make changes, because 2028 will be a presidential election year, in which Congress tends “not to do a lot,” he said.
“I would say the expectations for what Democrats can accomplish on healthcare should be tempered by the fact that President Trump will still be in the White House and has a veto pen,” he said. 
Levitt still expects Democrats to promptly tackle the core issues of Medicaid and ACA premiums. 
“I also expect President Trump to veto any bill that the Democrats pass to do this, if they are able to pass it,” Levitt said. “That takes us to the second path, which is kind of a game of 3D chess for Democrats to try to figure out what and how they can get President Trump to agree to restore some of these healthcare cuts.”
That could look like a delay of implementing ACA subsidy cuts or including Trump priorities such as health care savings accounts, he said. 
A third path could look like “populist healthcare ideas” that might pull in bipartisan support, such as addressing drug prices, which tends to be popular with both sides, price transparency and breaking up big insurance conglomerates. 
Amanda Seitz, Washington health policy reporter, said President Donald Trump shifted messaging several times in the first few days, appearing at times conciliatory and willing to work with Democrats, and then giving tours of his in-progress ballroom. 
She said it’s doubtful Trump will go along with reversing cuts to Medicaid. 
“Republicans really do view that as a signature achievement of this administration so far,” Seitz said. “However, I think we should be watching the rulemaking around Medicaid over the next couple weeks and months.”
The definition of Medicaid frailty is being challenged in court, and Medicaid work requirements are expected to go into effect Jan. 1. 
“There’s going to be a lot of pressure now on this administration to take a look at that again, especially when you have state legislatures that are now turning Democratic as well,” Seitz said. 
Democrats have created an 84-page working paper outlining healthcare policy, published by Politico in September, said Julie Rovner, chief Washington correspondent for KFF Health News. But she asked whether they have a plan to pay for what they outlined.  
Levitt said that’s typically the sticking point on any legislation, and healthcare changes will be no exception.
“We’re talking about almost a trillion dollars over 10 years in the Medicaid cuts, hundreds of billions of dollars for restoring the ACA premium subsidies, and I think that’s going to be a big fight,” he said. “Probably a big fight among Democrats, even whether they should try to pay for it. Republicans didn’t pay for all of the tax cuts they passed, and if this is a bill that the president is likely to veto anyway, why fight over how to pay for it?”
However, Levitt said, Democrats are unified on those issues, as well as reversing tax cuts for wealthy people. 
“That will be the first big fight, is whether Democrats pay for it, how they pay for it, and procedurally how they’re even going to proceed,” he said. 
Rovner asked how sure anyone is that Trump will veto such bills. 
“He’s obviously thinking about his legacy, and we know he likes to think about his legacy in terms of physical buildings like the ballroom and the reflecting pool,” she said. “Trump has proved very unpredictable in the past.”
Rovner pointed out that incoming senator from Michigan Abdul el-Sayed had said he’d be happy to name his health plan after Trump if it would get the president to sign it.
Levitt said he’s not sure Trump is particularly attached to Medicaid cuts. 
“He said during the 2024 campaign that he wasn’t going to cut Medicaid,” Levitt said. “He wasn’t going to cut Medicare, right? So I doubt that was a priority for him. I don’t think we can necessarily predict exactly what President Trump would do on the Affordable Care Act.”
There also could be a shift from Republicans left in Congress, as the ACA premiums affected middle-income people above four times the poverty level, such as farmers, ranchers and small-business owners, traditionally Republican constituencies, Levitt said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Two Kansas GOP legislative leaders accuse governor of misconduct in Walk of Honor selections
description: Two members of the Kansas Legislature allege Gov. Laura Kelly ignored state law by unilaterally selecting people to be added to the Capitol's Walk of Honor.
text:
Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly speaks Oct. 29, 2026, during a ceremony at the Capitol honoring eight people added to the Kansas Walk of Honor. Two Republican members of the Kansas Legislature claim she violated state law by unilaterally choosing eight new inductees. (Photo by Kansas Governor's Office)TOPEKA — The Republican House speaker and Senate majority leader Friday accused Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly of breaking Kansas law by personally selecting a group of people honored with bronze plaques at the Capitol.
Kelly, who completes her second term as governor in January, celebrated Oct. 29 the addition of seven women and one man to the Kansas Walk of Honor. The class included basketball pioneer James Naismith, educator Lucinda Todd, abolitionist Clarina Nichols and Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation Chairwoman Minnie Evans.
House Speaker Dan Hawkins and Senate Majority Leader Chase Blasi, both Wichita Republicans, said the governor failed to adhere to Kansas statute when she unilaterally chose honorees and directed placement of sidewalk markers without consulting the Kansas Legislature.
“The governor bypassed the statute and installed these unlawfully and, in addition, had a ceremony already,” Hawkins said.
Blasi, who serves on the Legislature’s capitol preservation committee, said he would welcome legal analysis of the governor’s actions. He suggested the joint preservation committee should be allowed to add its voice to discussion of memorials placed on the Capitol grounds “as the law requires.”
“The governor has decided to unlawfully violate the law and do whatever she wants,” he said.
Kelly’s staff didn’t respond to a request for comment, but she has said responsibility for selecting recipients fell to the state’s governors.
“The honorees being added to the Kansas Walk of Honor have always been an important part of Kansas history,” Kelly said in a statement last week. “They broke down barriers, challenged injustice, led industries and opened doors for generations to follow. Their contributions have shaped our state and our nation, which is why their names will forever be embedded in the sidewalks around the Statehouse, ensuring their stories live on in perpetuity.”
Kansas hasn’t applied a rigid selection formula or a mandatory legislative voting process for designation of these honorees. Since the Walk of Honor was established by GOP Gov. Sam Brownback in 2011, decisions involved the state’s governor in coordination with the Kansas Historical Society. The Kansas Historical Foundation finances the memorial plaques.
The governor was joined at last month’s ceremony on the Capitol steps by representatives of the Kansas Historical Society, Capitol Preservation Committee, family members of honorees and private donors to the project.
“Over the last 15 years, we have honored 17 Kansans from all walks of life who have made a significant impact on the state and to the country. We are pleased to include these eight new honorees,” said Patrick Zollner, executive director of the Kansas Historical Society.
The new honorees included Naismith, who invented basketball in 1891 and became the University of Kansas’ first head basketball coach. Todd, a civil rights advocate and teacher from Litchfield, was part of the families challenging school segregation in the landmark 1954 decision by the U.S. Supreme Court in Brown v. Topeka Board of Education.
Nichols was a women’s rights advocate who helped secure constitutional recognition of married women’s property rights and rights in child custody matters. Evans, who served as tribal chairwoman of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, defended tribal sovereignty and helped defeat federal efforts to terminate the standing of tribes, including the Potawatomi.
Kelly paid tribute to Georgia Neese Clark Gray, a Richland native and Washburn University graduate who became the first woman to serve as U.S. treasurer. She was appointed by President Harry Truman in 1949.
The governor selected for recognition Olive Ann Beech, an aviation executive from Waverly. She built Beech Aircraft into a major manufacturer and was the first woman to lead a Fortune 500 company.
Another addition was Mary Skubitz, a labor rights advocate who helped lead a 1921 march in which thousands of women joined striking coal miners protesting unfair labor practices in Kansas coalfields. The list included Kay McFarland, the first woman appointed to the Kansas Supreme Court and the first woman to serve as the Supreme Court’s chief justice.
Previously, Kelly selected U.S. Sen. Pat Roberts, who represented Kansas in Congress from 1981 to 2021.
Brownback, the Republican governor who created the Walk of Honor program, chose the 16 other people honored in this way. His list included 14 men and two women.
He started with U.S. Sen. Bob Dole in 2011, before selecting Vice President Charles Curtis, aviator Amelia Earhart and Nobel Prize winner Jack Kilby in 2012.
In 2015, Brownback’s list was expanded to aviation executive Clyde Cessna, automaker Walter Chrysler, physician Samuel Crumbine, artist John Steuart Curry, photographer Gordon Parks, journalist William Allen White and President Dwight Eisenhower.
In 2016, Brownback included entrepreneur Fred Harvey, U.S. Sen. Nancy Landon Kassebaum, Gov. Alf Landon, cattle transport executive Joseph McCoy and psychiatrist Carl Menninger.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Von Gillern concedes; jockeying begins for speakership of Nebraska Legislature
description: OMAHA — An incumbent state senator eyed as the frontrunner for speaker of the Nebraska Legislature has conceded his Omaha-area race in a rematch with his 2022 challenger. State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, in a statement Friday, congratulated state Sen.-elect Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha. Since joining the Legislature in 2023, von Gillern has served [[...]
text:
State Sen. Brad von Gillern and Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek are facing off again for to represent west-central Douglas County's Legislative District 4. They are pictured in Omaha in early October 2026. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — An incumbent state senator eyed as the frontrunner for speaker of the Nebraska Legislature has conceded his Omaha-area race in a rematch with his 2022 challenger.
State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, in a statement Friday, congratulated state Sen.-elect Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha. Since joining the Legislature in 2023, von Gillern has served in leadership positions for the Revenue Committee, including the first two years as vice chair to former state Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn before becoming chair.
“I wish Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek success as she heads to Lincoln to be our representative and will do all that I can to tee her up to succeed,” von Gillern wrote. “Her success is Nebraska’s success. The job is difficult and thankless, but vastly rewarding.”
State Sens. Rob Clements of Elmwood, left, and Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn talk with reporters after a meeting of the Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board at the Nebraska State Capitol on Oct. 30, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The Douglas County Election Commission released updated results 12:15 p.m. Friday with 8,000 more ballots counted (about 7,000 are left). In Legislative District 4, 645 more ballots were counted.
In the latest results, Maxwell-Ostdiek’s lead expanded by almost 80 votes. She leads with 9,099 votes (51%) to von Gillern’s 8,729 votes (49%). In 2022, von Gillern won the election with 8,710 votes, a margin of 4.8 percentage points over Maxwell-Ostdiek that year.
The New York Times has not yet called the LD 4 race for Maxwell-Ostdiek, nor the winners in three other legislative races (LD 14, LD 18 and LD 36). However, with von Gillern’s announcement, all four second-place finishers now have conceded. All newly elected lawmakers, including Maxwell-Ostdiek, have started new senator orientation, or “senator school,” already.
The Nebraska Board of State Canvassers, composed of State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg, Secretary of State Bob Evnen, Gov. Jim Pillen, Attorney General Mike Hilgers and Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley, meets to certify Nebraska’s May 12 primary election. At the podium, speaking to the board, is Deputy Secretary of State Wayne Bena. June 8, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Final results will be released in the coming weeks. The Nebraska Board of State Canvassers — consisting of the state’s constitutional officers — will finalize the election in early December.
Maxwell-Ostdiek also released a statement Friday saying she was “honored to have earned the trust of District 4 voters.”
“This campaign has been an unforgettable experience, and I am deeply grateful to everyone who helped make this victory possible,” Maxwell-Ostdiek wrote.
Speaker of the Legislature
Multiple lawmakers viewed von Gillern as the leading contender to succeed term-limited state Sen. John Arch of La Vista as speaker of the Legislature, a post he held for four years in turbulent times.
State Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, left, meets with State Sen. Paul Strommen of Sidney. March 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In Nebraska’s one-house Legislature, the speaker sets the daily debate schedule, and the speaker’s election is the first vote cast by senators each year. Under legislative rules, leadership votes are via secret ballot.
One lawmaker had already voiced her intention to seek the role regardless of von Gillern’s election: state Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha. Another, state Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, had said he would pursue the top role only if von Gillern lost. Jacobson has long said he wanted the Revenue Committee chairship but was willing to step up for speaker if needed.
The Nebraska Examiner can confirm one other legislator is considering the role: state Sen. Teresa Ibach of Sumner. Ibach said in the past 48 hours she’s had conversations with colleagues who encouraged her to seek the top spot, but she has not made a final call.
State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, center, meets with, from left, State Sens. Dave Murman of Glenvil, Barry DeKay of Niobrara, Steve Halloran of Hastings, Steve Erdman of Bayard and Brian Hardin of Gering. Feb. 23, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Kauth, Jacobson and Ibach all have legislative leadership positions already:

Kauth is chair of the Business and Labor Committee.
Jacobson is chair of the Banking, Commerce and Insurance Committee, and he is vice chair of the Revenue Committee.
Ibach is vice chair of the Executive Board (an internal high-ranking committee that handles day-to-day affairs of the legislative branch) and the Agriculture Committee.

Lawmakers have said other legislators have discussed or are looking for other names, too.
‘One of the best experiences of my life’
Von Gillern, in his concession, thanked his wife, Mary, for joining him in the campaign and service, describing her as an “integral part of this service to our great state.” He also extended his “deepest gratitude” to supporters, some of whom gave time, resources, prayers and encouragement.
“All of it mattered,” von Gillern said.
State Sen. Teresa Ibach of Sumner, center, talks with State Sen. Steve Erdman of Bayard. State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln watches to Ibach’s left. July 29, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Von Gillern said he launched his reelection bid one year ago to “finish the job,” including reforming the tax code, keeping neighborhoods safe and growing the economy. He said lawmakers “were able to accomplish a great deal” toward those efforts.
“Unfortunately, the voters wanted a change in this seat,” von Gillern wrote.
“I appreciate the feeling that tax relief did not replace the need and desire for tax reform,” von Gillern continued, “and I understand that national politics far from Nebraska increased the cost of goods we rely on right here in District 4.”
Von Gillern said he ran a positive and energetic race, worked his “tail off” each day to share his vision and knocked on close to 10,000 doors. He said he truly enjoyed talking with thousands of Nebraskans, including on porches where he said he earned some of his “fondest memories” that he’ll remember forever.
“It was an honor and one of the best experiences of my life,” von Gillern said. “I commit to wrap up the final days of my term just like the previous days, by working hard to ensure that this next 110th (Legislature) is productive and beneficial to Nebraskans.”
‘Earned the trust of District 4 voters’
Maxwell-Ostdiek thanked von Gillern for his “longstanding contributions to our community” as well as his legislative service. She said she wishes von Gillern and his wife well and looks forward to working with von Gillern during the transition.
Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha, a 2026 candidate for Legislative District 4, talks with volunteers for her campaign in her west Omaha neighborhood on Oct. 4, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The senator-elect will be the lone registered nonpartisan in the Legislature next year.
“(I) want to be clear that I intend to represent all of my District 4 neighbors, regardless of their party or who they supported this election season,” Maxwell-Ostdiek wrote.
“The voters of this district elected me because property taxes are too high, the cost of living is rising too quickly, the state is in a budget crisis and Nebraskans don’t feel heard,” she continued. “I will work every day to deliver progress on these issues, and look forward to getting started.”
